The one genuinely open interface is Open Sound Control, where a program on the same machine can set and read avatar values, push in gaze and body tracker poses and drive movement, with VRChat advertising itself for discovery over Zeroconf and asking the person's consent before it sends anything out. Two traps for a standards reader: the coordinate convention is left-handed with Y up, the opposite of the neutral transfer formats, and saved player data is forbidden by design from being shared between worlds, so a portal carries your account and your avatar and nothing else.

subjects.name: Open Metaverse Browser
subjects.summary: The Open Metaverse Browser is the Metaverse Standards Forum's own attempt at a neutral client for spatial content, and it is the only subject on this map that is a working browser with a downloadable binary and a documented module interface. Read the parts separately, because they are not governed alike. Sneeze, the engine, is Apache-2.0 and lives under the Forum's GitHub organisation; RCSF, a canonical skeleton mapping across fifteen formats, is Forum-hosted and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Everything else is Metaversal Corporation's: Rubidium, the browser you actually run, is proprietary with all rights reserved; the Halogen renderer, the RMAP networking library, the Map library and the WebAssembly SDKs are the vendor's repositories, and Sneeze pins all of them. SneezeSDK is the module-writing half of that split, and it is the only published contract this subject has: an Apache-2.0 C header that fixes the whole guest-to-engine wire format, a language-neutral reference with one page per class, and per-language bindings carried as submodules. It is not Forum-governed — it sits under MetaversalCorp — yet it is what a second implementer would have to build against, because the engine ships no specification of the fabric format. This file scores the SDK at its `prep` branch, head `4239e2b`, 18 August 2026. That branch differs from `main` in documentation only: it adds first-run guides for Linux, macOS and Windows, and it is behind `main` on the version file, on the versioning rule the front page used to state, and on four of the five binding pins. Count the bindings carefully — the front page marks five available, while the SDK's own reference and its porting guide both still say three. Three things a standards audience should not take on trust. Signature verification is called and its result thrown away, so an unverified fabric loads and runs; the trust level a module reads is then overwritten with a constant before it is stored, so it reports the same value whatever the certificate said. There is no resource budget at all, no fuel, no deadline and no memory ceiling, although the project's own wiki promises each fabric a CPU budget. And there is no format specification and no conformance suite, so the only definition of the format is the engine — and inside the SDK the C reference already contradicts the header it says it layers on, describing the fabric's services as an indexed list in the open snapshot where every other page says they are keyed by name and deliberately kept out of it. Whole planes are simply absent: no audio, no physics, no avatar, no geospatial anything, no credential of any kind, and immersive sessions are a runtime probe rather than a session. Buildable today from public sources: Sneeze, its SDKs and Halogen, pinned to public dependencies — except that Sneeze links the vendor's Map library, whose own README says it configures but does not yet compile, and which ships with no licence file at all.

subjects.name: RP1 Spatial Fabric
subjects.summary: RP1 Spatial Fabric is the idea that a place in three dimensions can be a document with a URL, the way a web page is, plus the stack that makes that real: a signed fabric file, a native engine that reads it, and a browser that opens it. The fabric file is a compact JSON Web Signature over a JSON manifest, signed RS256 against an X.509 chain carried in the header, listing WebAssembly modules that may be pinned by hash and a scene tree of packed 528-byte node records with 64-bit positions; a portal is simply a node with subtype 255 whose resource reference is the URL of another fabric, so fabrics nest and each nested one is verified on its own. Correction, dated 2026-09-03: this record previously said the browser had no public source and that two engine dependencies were private, which was true when it was observed on 2026-08-13 and is not true now; since 2026-09-01 the engine Sneeze, the browser Rubidium, the realtime library RMAP, the map library Map and the guest SDK are all public repositories, and the engine's dependency manifest clones the two former blockers from public addresses. Read the licences before reusing any of it: the engine, the SDK and RMAP are Apache-2.0, the browser's own README calls it proprietary with all rights reserved, and Map ships no licence file. The trap is smaller than it was but still the main one: there is now a published interface header the vendor calls the canonical frozen contract, but there is still no fabric-file specification and no conformance suite, so compatible with this format has no testable meaning, and three incompatible manifest dialects still ship together inside one public repository at one commit, including a signed sample whose payload disagrees with the unsigned source file beside it. Signing works and is stable, but signature acceptance is not scene compatibility, and the vendor's own documentation records that the browser currently pins the trust level instead of acting on the one it computed.

subjects.name: TeleportXR
subjects.summary: TeleportXR is a session protocol, not a document format. A server runs the live simulation and holds the truth of it; each client receives only the partial, temporary slice of state it needs right now. Three transports run in parallel: a WebSocket for signalling, WebRTC data channels and media tracks for real-time data and audio, and plain HTTP for static assets. Its own documentation states that Teleport has no file format and that the Teleport network is part of the Internet but not part of the Web. It is by some distance the most completely specified subject in this group at the session layer, and it is the only one here that states its unit: linear units are metres, and handedness and vertical axis are negotiated rather than assumed. Between 2026-06-16 and 2026-09-03 the identity gap that used to define this subject was largely filled, in the reference implementations first and the specification second. An avatar offer may now carry the address of a signed Universal Manifest instead of a bare asset URL; the server verifies Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON, gates each facet against the subject's own consent records with default-deny, and returns a structured receipt. Separately the connect message's identity member, still documented as an opaque string, is implemented as a structured identity with three trust levels and a challenge-response that binds an OpenID Connect token to a client-held key. Three cautions. The chapter that would specify the manifest mechanism, avatar_manifest, is referenced from three places and is not in the public repository. Verification is explicitly not proof of the bearer's right to the document, and only trust tier zero is supported. And watch the word Node: a TeleportXR node is a changing object inside a live stream with no URL, which is not what the same word means in a world-addressing API.

subjects.name: Vibe Jam portal convention
subjects.summary: The Vibe Jam portal convention is a small informal rule set, published by the organiser of the Vibe Jam game competition, for linking browser games into a webring. A game may place an exit portal that sends the player to a Vibe Jam address, which forwards them to a randomly chosen participating game, and a game that receives a player places a return portal to the game they came from. The player's name, colour, speed, direction of travel, rotation, health, team and an avatar link ride along as optional values in the web address so the next game can place the player with continuity. It covers the hop itself and nothing else: there is no identity check, no agreed format for what the avatar link points to, no state beyond the listed values and no way to name a chosen destination, and everything about rendering, physics, sensing and capture is left to each game. Trap for a standards audience: it is a page of prose plus one sample script, not a versioned specification, all values travel unauthenticated in plain web addresses to whichever game comes next, and the sample return code navigates to whatever address the incoming ref value names.

subjects.name: Web of Worlds
subjects.summary: Web of Worlds is a Metaverse Standards Forum direction for making virtual worlds addressable and linkable with ordinary web machinery, announced by the Forum's 3D Web Interoperability Working Group on 2 June 2026. Its whole normative surface is three small OpenAPI files at version 0.0.1 — a world API, an asset API and a user manifest API — plus a README table of five core requirements saying a world is joined, followed, previewed, saved and shared by its URL. It is strong on one idea, that a world is a URL and its parts hang off that URL, and it does that well. Almost everything else a working group would look for is absent rather than wrong: no units, no scale, no up axis, no bounds, no coordinate reference system, no signature, no destination on a portal, and no way for one world to contain another. The first trap is that none of the three files uses a single normative keyword and no schema requires a single property, so an empty object validates as a World, a User, a Node, a Portal, a View and a Spatial descriptor alike; a team that reads the whitepaper will expect decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, selective disclosure, glTF, USD and X3D, and will find none of them in the machine-readable text. The second trap is now demonstrated rather than predicted: the world README puts the scene graph under /wow/scene/, the machine-readable file puts it under /wow/spatial/{spatialID}, and the project's own reference implementation, simpleWorlds, publishes a third OpenAPI file that serves /wow/scene/node/{nodeId}. The specification and its reference implementation disagree about the normative graph path, so two good-faith servers cannot talk.

subjects.name: C2PA Content Credentials
subjects.summary: Content Credentials record who made a piece of content and what was done to it, as signed statements bound to the bytes of the file. It is deployed rather than proposed: there is a conformance programme, a public list of conforming products, a published certificate policy and a curated list of trusted signing authorities. Two things a spatial computing group needs to know. First, no three-dimensional asset format appears anywhere in its list of supported formats, so a model cannot carry an embedded manifest at all; the byte-range binding works on any file, but the record has to travel beside the file as a separate manifest, and nothing keeps the two together. Second, the two pieces people most often credit to it are not in it: the verifiable credentials section and the training and data mining assertion were both removed from the core in version 2.0 of January 2024, and now live as separate specifications of another organisation. It records provenance; it does not enforce a licence, and its own principles say it passes no judgement on what it reports.

subjects.name: Decentralized Identifiers
subjects.summary: A decentralized identifier gives a person, an agent or a thing a name that its own controller holds, rather than one an account provider issues. The core specification is a finished web recommendation from July 2022 and it covers three things well: the shape of the identifier, the document it resolves to, and which key may be used for which purpose. It deliberately stops short of everything after that. It carries no claims about a person, no protocol for handing credentials over, and it states that what happens once an identifier holder has proved control is left to each method and each application. Two traps for a working group: the newer revision is not finished, having sat at candidate stage since March 2026 past the earliest date it could have advanced; and no concrete method is standardized at all, with 269 of them listed, as of 7 September 2026, in a group note that says in its own words that listing is not endorsement.

subjects.name: IEEE 2874 Spatial Web
subjects.summary: This is a reference model, not something an engineer can build against yet: its own project record says it provides a reference model and defines requirements for a set of implementation specifications still to be developed, and the foundation that wrote the base document lists those implementation standards as under development. The catalogue abstract is ambitious - a layer stack, a spatial range query format, a data ontology, a credentialing method for granting access, and a contracting language that can execute obligations automatically - and it is the one clause in that list that claims terms can be acted on rather than merely recorded. Board approval on 28 May 2025 is confirmed, but the catalogue title still reads approved draft standard, so say board-approved and give no publication date. The register its naming would need does not exist, and the project record says the foundation was still working out with the registration authority how to build it. The identifier method its originators say the system will use, did:swid, is not among the 267 methods listed in the web consortium's register. The text is behind a paywall, so every row here is marked reported rather than verified: none of it comes from the normative text.

subjects.name: Inter-World Portaling System
subjects.summary: The Inter-World Portaling System is OMA3's draft protocol for one narrow job, moving a person from one virtual world to another, and it does that job with two calls over ordinary web protocols. A query call, made on the public link a world advertises, asks the destination may I come in and returns an approval, an address to teleport to, an approved landing spot, an optional link for downloading the destination's client and a number of seconds before the approval lapses; a teleport call then executes the move, launches the destination client, shows the person a two-digit number so they can confirm they arrived where they meant to, and calls back a success or failure address on the source side. It invents no address scheme of its own and defines a genuine resolution step, which is more than most portal proposals manage, and its drafting discipline is strong: defined modal verbs, requirement tables marked mandatory, optional, excluded or conditional, an explicit clause on what claiming conformance obliges you to support, and a forward-compatibility rule for reserved fields. The traps are large: the place inside the address is an optional free-text field whose form the destination world decides, so the only published design that resolves a portal does not standardize the name inside it; the three things it is most often credited with, asset transfer, look and feel negotiation and payments, are each a single line reading to be decided, with the field that would carry an avatar marked reserved for future use in both calls; and the websocket option in the address format is left undecided as well. The normative text is damaged in places too: the query response table lists the success callback twice where the second should be the failure callback, three steps name fields that appear in no table, and one step points at a Section 7.8 in a document that ends at Section 6. There is nothing here to build against yet, with version 0.3 appearing only as a file name on a PDF, no tag, no release, no reference implementation and no commit to the specification since September 2025.

subjects.name: JSON-LD 1.1
subjects.summary: JSON-LD 1.1 is the World Wide Web Consortium format for writing Linked Data, meaning facts about things and their relationships, in ordinary JSON. It covers well the naming of things by web address, the mapping of short property names to shared vocabularies through a context, and the conversion of one document between compact, expanded and flattened forms. It leaves to others every domain meaning: geometry, scenes, identity proofs, licences, networking and rendering all need a vocabulary or a separate specification layered on top. A trap for a standards audience is that a processor silently drops any property its context does not map to a web address, so two systems with different contexts can read the same file and see different data. A second is that remote contexts are fetched by address, so a document's meaning can change or fail to load unless the context is pinned or cached.

subjects.name: MPEG-I Avatar Representation Format
subjects.summary: A draft international standard for carrying a person's avatar between applications. It is not finished. The standards catalogue still lists it as a draft that reached the stage where the draft ballot passed on 2026-07-31, its own group calls that the move to the final draft stage, and the group expects publication at the beginning of 2027. Nothing here should be described as settled behaviour. What it defines is a data model, several containers, a sample format for animation, a stream format, a way to sit inside the group's own scene description, and mechanisms meant to show that an avatar is genuine. Two points matter for a standards audience. First, it does not name its own bones or expressions: it points at outside animation frameworks by name, and the worked examples point at one headset maker's body and face tracking, so the agreement that makes an avatar portable is borrowed rather than made here. Second, it is not the first formal standard to claim avatar portability. A 2016 international standard from the same committee already says its job is letting a virtual object or its characteristics move from one virtual world to another. Note the evidence limit: the normative text is sold, not published, and we did not read it, so every row is marked reported.

subjects.name: MPEG-I Immersive Audio
subjects.summary: A finished international standard for immersive sound in virtual and augmented spaces, published on 2025-11-03 as edition 1.0. It models sound sources together with the space around them, covering reverberation, early reflections, occlusion, bending of sound around edges and pitch shift from movement, with the listener free to both turn and walk, and it carries all of that in a compressed stream. Its own listening test, run across six laboratories and reported in January 2026, placed it in the excellent band at a middle score of 84 out of 100, so saying nobody is working on spatial sound is false. Be clear about the evidence here: the normative text is sold, not published, and we did not read it. Every row below rests on the publisher's catalogue record, the group's own standard page, its own white paper and its own test report, so every row is marked reported rather than verified. The trap worth taking to a working group is that it needs the scene geometry a second time, in its own encoder input format, so a world that already describes its walls for pictures must describe them again for sound.

subjects.name: MPEG-I Scene Description
subjects.summary: A published international standard, now in its second edition as ISO/IEC 23090-14:2025, that defines no scene format of its own. Its abstract says so plainly: it specifies extensions to existing scene description formats, and those extensions are provided for ISO/IEC 12113 - which is glTF 2.0 - so the earlier reading was right on both counts, extensions to an existing format plus a media access interface between the part of a client that renders and the part that fetches. What it brings to a scene is timed media: video as a texture, spatial audio with reverb, buffers that keep refilling, scene updates arriving as samples, a director's viewpoint that moves, and a way to wrap a glTF scene and its media inside a media file. On avatars the earlier reading needs splitting in two - an in-scene humanoid model did land in this standard, through the amendment on haptics, augmented reality, avatars, interactivity and lighting that was folded into the second edition, while the portable avatar exchange format is a separate part, ISO/IEC 23090-39, still a draft and not published. On world-to-world transfer the earlier reading should be corrected: this standard does not cover it and neither does any other part of this forty-part family; the nearest, Part 28, is asset interchange, not moving a user or their state. Two traps for a standards audience: the second edition is published but the MPEG_ extensions sitting in the glTF extension registry are still the first edition's, with the second edition's registration still a draft agenda item at the July 2026 meeting; and because this standard extends glTF 2.0 while Khronos is revising the glTF core in 2.1, the two overlap across the whole asset side - glTF owns the container, geometry, materials and animation, this standard owns timed media on top - with interactivity now being specified twice, here through the folded amendment and at Khronos through KHR_interactivity.

subjects.name: MPEG-I Visual Volumetric Video-based Coding (V3C, V-PCC and MIV)
subjects.summary: One bitstream, two halves, two working groups. Visual volumetric video-based coding is the shared format: it cuts a volumetric frame into patches, projects them onto flat planes, and codes the resulting occupancy, geometry and attribute pictures with an ordinary video codec - AVC, HEVC or VVC - while a small atlas of patch descriptions says how to put the points back in space. Video-based point cloud compression is one application of it, an annex of the same part, owned by the 3D graphics group; MPEG immersive video is the other, a separate part that normatively references the shared format and extends it, owned by the video coding group. The published state is edition 3 of Part 5 in March 2025 and edition 2 of Part 12 in September 2025, with conformance and reference software for the immersive half published in 2026 and the reference encoder public under a BSD licence. What it covers: volumetric video, end to end and seriously - profiles, tiers, six levels, two named conformance points, and a real camera model for multi-camera capture with perspective, equirectangular and orthographic projections. What it leaves to others: everything a world needs. It has no scene graph, no scripting, no identity, no networking session, no anchors and no audio; those rows are honestly out of scope, not missing. Four traps for a standards audience. First, handedness: the frame that patches reconstruct into is described as left-handed, opposite to glTF, OpenUSD and every web runtime on this map, and the block that could name the axis convention is optional and often absent. Second, the standard does not deliver itself - storage in the ISO base media file format and transport over adaptive streaming are Part 10, a different part, so any claim that this format streams is really a claim about its neighbour. Third, meshes: the scope names mesh representations as a target of the generic mechanism, but no mesh coding is published here; that is Part 29, still in development, and the planned fourth edition of Part 5 is what folds it in. Fourth, splats: a first amendment to this part that would add Gaussian splat coding through the same video-based framework has been promoted, and MPEG has an open exploration with a call for content dated July 2026, so the row that reads empty today is the row most likely to change next. One more thing a reader should know: the published text sits behind ISO's paywall, so every quote in this file comes from MPEG's own freely published documents - the 2020 final draft of Part 5, the approved white papers of 2021 and 2026, the standards pages, and the public reference software. Where a fact could have changed between the 2020 draft and the published editions, the note says which document it came from.

subjects.name: Model Context Protocol
subjects.summary: The Model Context Protocol is an open protocol that lets applications built around language models connect to outside data sources and tools. It covers how a client and a server agree on a version, discover each other's features, exchange messages over standard input and output or over web requests, expose data, prompts and tools, and ask a user for input, with an optional sign-in flow built on OAuth for web use. Its optional extensions add interactive web interfaces shown inside a conversation, and the project also runs a public registry of servers. It leaves everything about three-dimensional content, avatars, capture, rendering, physics, geographic positioning, shared worlds and portable identity credentials to other standards. A trap for standards audiences: version 2026-07-28 dropped the session handshake and protocol-level sessions, so sources describing earlier versions are out of date, and its sign-in model grants access to a server on a user's behalf rather than carrying verifiable claims about a person or agent.

subjects.name: OAuth 2.0 with protected-resource metadata
subjects.summary: OAuth 2.0 is the Internet Engineering Task Force framework by which an application obtains limited access to a web service, either with the approval of the person who owns the data or on its own behalf; Request for Comments 6749 defines it and Request for Comments 9728 adds a standard way for a protected service to publish what a client needs to know, such as which authorization servers it trusts and which scope values it accepts. It covers delegation well: scoped, time-limited access tokens, a refresh path, registries for extensions, and discovery of the authorization server for a service the client already knows. It leaves to others the token format, how a service checks tokens with the authorization server, how clients register, how a person is signed in, and everything about the content and behaviour of worlds. A standards audience should know that the framework itself warns it is likely to produce non-interoperable implementations unless profiles fix its optional parts, so saying a system supports OAuth does not tell two systems they will work together. It also authorizes access without authenticating anyone or saying who they are, and its discovery begins only once the client already knows the service address.

subjects.name: OGC 3D Tiles (Community Standard)
subjects.summary: Streaming very large three-dimensional geospatial data by tile, and the only thing on this map that solves that problem in a ratified document. Two facts about its standing are easy to get wrong. It is an OGC Community Standard, not an OGC Implementation Standard, submitted by a single company and approved on that basis; and it was approved 2022-12-17 and published 2023-01-12, not in 2025. Its document address lives under the community-standard path, and the implementation-standard path returns nothing. What it actually specifies is a tree of tiles with an error measure and a refinement rule, a coordinate reference frame, structured metadata and a small styling language. What it deliberately does not specify is the model itself: since version 1.1 the tile payload is the common asset format, and its own four original tile formats are deprecated. Two traps. Its up axis is not the same as that format's, so a transform is applied on every tile. And its security section reads, in full, that no security considerations have been made.

subjects.name: OGC GeoPose
subjects.summary: OGC GeoPose is a small, finished standard that does one job: say where something is on Earth and which way it is facing, in a form two systems can exchange. The document records an approval date of 2022-06-20 and a publication date of 2023-09-08, so calling it a draft seeking uplift, as our own older research did, is wrong. It is a data structure and not a service: the word resolve does not appear anywhere in it, and it states plainly that it does not constrain services or interfaces, so it never turns a name into a place you can reach. Its two simple forms pin the outer frame to the world geodetic system of 1984, while the flexible form only names an outside frame authority and says reading that name is somebody else's job, so two systems can exchange a valid pose and still disagree about where it is. One trap for anyone citing it: the published rule for latitude reads that the minimum value shall be 90.0 degrees and the maximum value shall be 90.0 degrees, with the minus sign missing, while the neighbouring rule for longitude correctly carries its minus sign.

subjects.name: OMI glTF extensions
subjects.summary: The Open Metaverse Interoperability Group's glTF extensions are a public collection of draft add-ons to the Khronos glTF 2.0 asset format, aimed at features that virtual worlds need and the base format lacks. At the pinned commit the repository holds thirteen of the group's own extensions (rigid-body physics with shapes, joints and gravity volumes; four vehicle parts; seats and spawn points for characters; a sky and environment-light definition; and two audio codec add-ons) plus the text of the Khronos positional audio extension, which has since graduated to Khronos. It covers world-level physics and character placement well, in a form several game engines can already map onto their own systems. It leaves nearly everything else to others: mesh, texture and material encoding stay with glTF itself, and networking, identity, capture, sensing and delivery belong to other standards. Traps for a standards audience: no extension has passed the group's second maturity stage, so none is ratified, and most entries in the repository's own support table are marked unsupported; the physics extensions depend on each other and do nothing alone; and the proposals for world links and for character personality are archived, not current.

subjects.name: Open AR Cloud (Open Spatial Computing Platform)
subjects.summary: Open AR Cloud is a volunteer-run association that publishes the Open Spatial Computing Platform: a set of protocols and reference services for finding out where you are, finding what services and content are near you, and addressing a place so another system can reach it. Its strongest work is the part almost nothing else on this map covers. It gives every anchor, service and content bundle a stable address under a domain name authority with a normative resolution order and a required web fallback, which is the resolution step the OGC geospatial pose standard explicitly leaves out; it defines a request and response for recovering a pose from camera imagery and ships an open implementation of it; and it treats durable, shared, world-locked anchors as a first-class thing to publish and update. It is not a runtime and does not pretend to be. There is no rendering, no material, no animation, no avatar, no physics and no sound anywhere in it; the word avatar and the word physics occur nowhere in the current specification, and the only occurrence of audio is a Python package name in a build file. It does not hold content either: its own documentation says the platform connects users to resources operated by content providers, so licence terms, rights enforcement and delivery guarantees all sit outside it. The map should know that the platform is really two generations of work under one name. The original services, spatial service discovery and spatial content discovery, are web interfaces at version 1.0 over a peer-to-peer log database, and the reference client that uses them still describes the platform as an early prototype. SpatialDDS, the 2026 protocol, is a much larger specification over the OMG data bus, at version 1.7 dated 2026-08-23, with a 1.8 draft in the same repository; its own versioning clause suspends backward compatibility for the whole 1.x series and 1.7 broke the wire in eleven places. Its conformance appendix tests whether public datasets map onto the schema, and states plainly that it does not test interoperability between implementations. Two traps for anyone citing this subject. The association's public timeline claims a GeoPose 1.0 standard release in 2021 and a ratified spatial content discovery protocol in 2023, and neither claim is supported by a primary source: the OGC standard records approval in 2022 and publication in 2023, and the content discovery repository still calls its record format a base version expected to evolve. The same timeline claims an OSCP 3.0 released in 2024 with full edge computing support, and no specification, tag or repository for any such release exists in the association's public code. Take the repositories and the specification text over the website.

subjects.name: OpenUSD Core Specification
subjects.summary: The machinery for combining a scene out of many files is standardized. What you put inside the scene is not. The alliance behind it has published exactly one document, the core, version 1.0.1, dated 2025-12-12, and its own public repository lists that single row under available specifications. The core covers data types, the layer document model, paths, resource resolution, composition, value resolution, schemas, colour, collections and three file formats. It excludes geometry, materials and physics by name, and the words geometry and physics each appear exactly once in the whole document, in the sentence that excludes them. Two things a standards audience should carry away. First, the only schemas the core normatively defines are colour and collections, so there is no agreed way to say how big something is or which way is up. Second, the document is published under a licence that forbids distributing derivative works, which constrains how another standards body can build on it. Cite version 1.0.1 and the date: there is no 1.0.0.

subjects.name: OpenXR
subjects.summary: The settled way for an application to talk to a headset or a pair of glasses: it covers the session, the frame loop, the tracked spaces, the views to draw, the input actions and touch feedback. It is a ratified Khronos standard with a real conformance test suite and an adopter programme, and the current release is 1.1.63, dated 2 September 2026, so read the version line before you cite it. There are two builds of the same document: one with all ratified extensions and one with all registered extensions, and the second says of itself that it is not a ratified specification. Of the 253 extensions in the registry only 52 are ratified, all 29 Khronos-tagged ones and 23 of the 39 multi-vendor ones, and not one single-vendor extension is ratified. It draws nothing itself: an application cannot even open a session without one of the ratified graphics binding extensions, and there is no sound, no scene, no networking and no identity anywhere in it. Two traps for a standards audience: the nine ratified spatial extensions, the first six of them ratified in June 2025, give you anchors, planes, markers and persistence but no way to share an anchor with another device or another person, and the only two audio extensions in the whole registry are single-vendor and unratified, so the ratified specification has no audio surface at all.

subjects.name: SpatialDDS
subjects.summary: SpatialDDS is an open protocol, published as a draft by the Open AR Cloud association, for sharing live spatial information between robots, vehicles, phones, sensors and digital twins. It builds on the Object Management Group's Data Distribution Service, a publish-and-subscribe messaging standard, and defines typed messages for poses, coordinate frames, anchors, maps, sensor streams, detections, zones and events, with discovery by place and web-readable manifests. It covers positioning, frames, discovery, anchors and sensor data in depth, and it carries large content such as meshes and splats by reference rather than defining those formats. It leaves rendering, avatars, audio, physics, scripting, payments and scene graphs to others, and its own text says its subject is observations and predictions about the physical world. A standards audience should know that version 1.8 is a draft in which any minor release may still break the wire format before formal adoption, and that the Neural, Agent and Open World Model profiles that look closest to metaverse needs are informative or provisional examples outside the normative text.

subjects.name: SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC)
subjects.summary: The SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog is a community specification for describing and searching files that represent the Earth at a place and time, such as satellite and drone imagery, elevation models and lidar point clouds. It defines small catalogue, collection and item records that point to the files and carry a footprint, a time, a licence and descriptive properties, and it can be extended with named add-ons; a companion web interface specification adds search by place, time and collection. It covers discovery, coverage, licence, versioning and descriptive metadata of geospatial data well. It does not define how any asset is encoded or drawn, and it has nothing on scenes, avatars, identity, networking or sessions, which it leaves to the file formats it points to and to other standards. A standards audience should know that the search interface specification is versioned separately (1.0.0) from the core specification (1.1.0), and that useful fields for point clouds and tiling live in community extensions of varying maturity, with the tiling one still at proposal stage. A catalogue entry tells a client that a point cloud or three-dimensional file exists and where; it does not guarantee that a spatial runtime can load it.

subjects.name: Universal Manifest
subjects.summary: Universal Manifest is a portable signed identity envelope: a JSON-LD document carrying who a person, agent or device is, what they consent to, and pointers to the heavier things they own, signed with a profile called Signature Profile A. That profile is Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON with the signature member removed, and the key is named by a URI reference that must resolve. The envelope never hosts anything; pointers exist so that heavy files stay where they are. Around that core sits a published document set: a primer, a Tier-0/Tier-1 base specification, three tier extensions, an optional-features profile and a cookbook, with per-version conformance fixtures. Version 0.3 is named as the stable published reference and 0.4 as the production-candidate milestone, dated 9 July 2026, under the W3C Software and Document Licence with the Universal Manifest Working Group as editors. It is the only subject in this group with both a written specification and a real conformance suite, and the project's own implementation verifies byte for byte against the reference validators. Three things a standards audience should hold onto. First, the base is a boundary model: six stages run on arrival, a receipt is written, and nothing re-checks during a live session; the bilateral session model is published as preview. Second, the previous claim that nobody outside this stack had adopted it is no longer true, and this is the largest change in this file: the public TeleportXR repositories accept a Universal Manifest address in place of an avatar URL, verify Signature Profile A, gate each facet on the subject's consent with default-deny, and return a receipt. Third, only trust tier zero, signature-only, is verified by that implementation, and verification is explicitly not proof that the presenter is the subject.

subjects.name: VRM
subjects.summary: VRM is a humanoid avatar format built on glTF 2.0: a VRM file is a binary glTF file with one added extension and a changed file suffix, so everything the base format settles about meshes, textures and skins is inherited unchanged. What VRM adds is the part that makes an avatar work in a place it was not made for, and the base format has none of it: a fixed set of 55 named human bones with fixed parentage, 15 of them required; a normative rest pose that fixes which way the model faces and puts the soles on the ground plane at zero; and 18 named facial expressions covering five moods, five mouth shapes for speech, three eye closings and four gaze directions. It also carries permission data, which no other asset format on this map does, with required author names, a required link to the VRM Public License, and eleven machine-readable settings covering who may wear the model, commercial use, credit, modification, redistribution and violent, sexual, political or hateful content, every one of them defaulting to the restrictive value. Three traps for a standards audience: the expression names are agreed but the faces are not, because the specification says plainly that there is no specification for the facial deformation itself, so the same named expression need not look alike on two models; a VRM file carries no animation at all, because the core declares the base format's animation and camera arrays unused and puts humanoid motion in a separate file defined by a separate extension; and there is nothing for worn items, no attachment point, no socket and no way to reference a second file, so clothing has to be baked into the avatar mesh before export. Version 1.0 is the current one, released in September 2022; the older 0.x line used a different and incompatible extension key and is now deprecated.

subjects.name: Verifiable Credentials Data Model
subjects.summary: A verifiable credential is a signed statement made by one party about a subject that a third party can check without asking the first party. The data model became a full web recommendation on 15 May 2025, and six companion recommendations were published the same day: two ways of securing a credential, the two signature suites, EdDSA and ECDSA, that the first of those uses, a status format for withdrawing one, and a controlled identifier document format. What it does not do is move a credential between two parties. No finished recommendation defines that exchange, and the specification only observes, in a section it marks non-normative, that its roles suggest where such protocols would go. Two things a standards audience should hold on to: it does not require decentralized identifiers, only web addresses, so the two families are often paired by habit rather than by rule; and selective disclosure is a property of the chosen securing mechanism, which means the issuer has to enable it at issuing time and the holder cannot add it later.

subjects.name: Verse
subjects.summary: Verse is Epic Games' programming language for gameplay, the one Unreal Editor for Fortnite runs and the one Epic says its future engine will use. It is a subject on this map because of what it says about code, not about content: every function declares in its own signature what it may do — read memory, write it, fail, suspend, or run on the client ahead of the server — and the compiler enforces that declaration; state changed inside a failing branch is rolled back automatically; concurrency is in the language itself, with expressions that run several things at once, race them, or let one outlive its scope; and every published module has a permanent address that nobody else may ever claim. The row that should interest a standards group most is versioning: compatibility here is not a convention but a rule checked when code is published — a public definition can never be removed, renamed or changed in kind, and effects may only ever be dropped, never added — which is enforcement rather than policy, and is the one mechanism here a working group could copy rather than merely record. Everything about scenes, geometry, avatars, audio, positioning and devices is out of scope: this is a language, and its reference specifies none of it. Two traps. First, portability: the language reference is published under a public-domain dedication and is genuinely open to read, but the only implementation is a virtual machine held in a repository Epic has not published, so Verse code cannot be run, checked or replayed anywhere except inside Epic's own service — the 594 executable tests that ship with the reference cannot be run without Epic's binaries. Second, the reference documents the head of a development branch, so several things it describes in full — client prediction, reactive live variables, serialisation of saved data — are marked in the text itself as not yet released, and a reader who scores from the prose alone will credit Verse with features nobody can use today.

subjects.name: WebAssembly
subjects.summary: WebAssembly is a compact, safe and portable binary code format with a precisely defined instruction set and execution rules; it is a target that many programming languages compile to, not a format for scenes, avatars or media. It covers the safe running of untrusted code well: modules are validated before use, run isolated from their host, and can reach the outside world only through functions the host chooses to supply. It also has a strong change story: a backward-compatibility promise, a version field, ignorable custom sections for extensions, named language subsets including a deterministic one, and a public conformance test suite. It leaves everything about worlds to others: scenes, avatars, networking, identity, sensing, rendering, and even input and output, because the core specification defines no way to talk to any environment and leaves that to separate interface documents for each hosting environment. Trap for a standards audience: two hosts can run the same module only if both supply the same imports, so the claim that a platform runs WebAssembly says nothing about whether guest content written for another platform will work there. The address ending in wasm-core-2 now serves release 3.0 of the core specification, not release 2.0.

subjects.name: WebGPU
subjects.summary: A low level interface that lets a web page drive the graphics processor for drawing and for general computation, designed to map onto the native driver interfaces used on Windows, Apple platforms and Vulkan. It is not finished. Both the main specification and its separate shading language specification are Candidate Recommendation Drafts, both dated 15 September 2026, and the last formally reviewed snapshot of each is 19 December 2024, so no one should cite it as a completed recommendation. What it covers is draw pipelines, compute pipelines, buffers, textures, samplers, command queues, and a system of named optional features and numeric limits that an application must ask for and check. What it leaves to others is everything above that line: no materials, no lighting, no scene tree, no mesh or animation format, no physics, no sound, no networking, no anchors and no input devices. The trap for a spatial computing audience is that this interface cannot yet draw into an immersive session at all, because the binding that would join it to the immersive web interface is an editor's draft that has never been published on the technical reports track, so immersive web content still draws through the older web graphics interface.

subjects.name: WebXR Device API
subjects.summary: The way a web page reaches a headset or a phone's pass-through camera: it covers starting and ending an immersive session, the tracked spaces, the viewer's pose, the views to draw, the input sources and the frame loop. It is not finished. The core document is a Candidate Recommendation Draft dated 9 June 2026, and no part of this family has ever reached full Recommendation, so nobody should describe it as a completed web standard. Read it as a core plus a fan of modules that sit at very different stages: only the augmented reality module has reached candidate stage alongside the core, seven more are Working Drafts, and the anchors, plane detection and graphics binding documents are editor's drafts that have never been published on the technical reports track at all. It draws nothing itself and binds only to the older web graphics interface; the document that would let it use the newer one is one of those unpublished editor's drafts. Two traps for a standards audience: anchors can be made to survive a restart on the same device and the same site, but there is no way to share one with another device or another person and the word share does not appear in the anchors document at all, and there is no eye tracking module of any kind, so the gaze value in the core is head direction rather than eye direction.

subjects.name: X3D (ISO/IEC 19775-1)
subjects.summary: The oldest thing on this map and by far the widest. A published international standard, fourth edition, whose forty-two clauses already contain most of what newer formats are still drafting: rigid body physics with six joint types, spatialized sound with room acoustics, a human skeleton standard, text with fonts, volume rendering, shader bindings, a geospatial component with real coordinate reference frames, an event model for interactivity, a scripting component, and a networked component that shares entity state over a long-established simulation protocol. It also carries a proper conformance clause, which almost nothing else here does. Levels below say native for anything defined in a clause of this standard, since components are how this standard is built; where support depends on which profile a reader implements, the note says so. Three warnings for a standards audience. Its coverage is wide but its adoption is thin, so a cell being filled here does not mean two shipping products interoperate. Its unit of length can be changed by the file, unlike the common asset format, which fixes metres. And its addressing points at a file, not at a shared place, so two people opening the same address get two private copies.

subjects.name: glTF
subjects.summary: The settled way to hand a three-dimensional model from one tool to another. Everything about the shape of a thing and how its surface looks is finished, ratified and in the core: meshes, textures, a physically based material model, animation curves, skinning, morph targets, cameras, metres and a fixed axis convention. Everything about how a thing behaves is not. The whole specification text contains the word physics once, as a made-up name in an example, and the word audio zero times. Extensions carry the rest, so the level here follows a rule: native means the ratified core text, via-extension means a named extension the Khronos board has actually ratified, and partial means a named extension whose draft text is public but which is not ratified. Twenty-seven extensions are ratified, twenty-four from Khronos and three multi-vendor, and KHR_interactivity is among them. Physics and audio are not. One trap for a standards audience: this format has skins and joints but no agreed bone names, so an animation authored for one avatar will not play on another without a convention this specification does not supply.

subjects.name: glTF 2.1
subjects.summary: A planned backward-compatible revision of the glTF core, announced on 2026-06-11 and still being written. Its purpose is to let one file deliver a whole assembled scene instead of a single model: a file may reference other glTF files and instantiate them, package them inside itself, carry simple shapes such as boxes and spheres, and hang bounding volumes on nodes. Seven of the announced features have draft specification text - those four, plus thumbnails, the 64-bit binary container and the deprecation of multiple scenes, merged on 2026-08-28 - and only on the working group's draft-2.1 branch; the published Khronos registry still has no 2.1 document, and no primary source states a ratification target date. Everything else on the announced list - unique identifiers, promoted extensions and wider number types - is announced only, and is scored partial here for that reason. The shape work is the one to watch: the same box, sphere, capsule, cylinder and plane vocabulary that the physics and collision extensions were going to supply now sits in the core, and the working group has stated that the pending KHR_implicit_shapes extension is superseded by it - though that extension's pull request is still open and the extension registry has not been changed to say so. This is also the format that the international scene description standard extends: MPEG-I Scene Description, ISO/IEC 23090-14:2025, defines no scene format of its own and states in its own abstract that its extensions are provided for ISO/IEC 12113, which is glTF 2.0 - so the two overlap across the whole asset side, with glTF owning the container, geometry, materials and animation and the MPEG part owning timed media on top, and with interactivity now being defined twice, once by each body. Those MPEG extensions are pinned to glTF 2.0, so a core revision is something that standard has to catch up with rather than something it inherits.

subjects.name: 4D Gaussian splatting and splat formats
subjects.summary: Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting is a way of representing a captured place as millions of small, semi-transparent, oriented ellipsoids, each carrying a size, an orientation, an opacity and a set of spherical-harmonic colour terms, drawn by sorting them and blending them rather than by shading surfaces; the four-dimensional work extends it to moving scenes. This record scores the technique together with the file formats that carry it, because for a standards audience the formats are the interoperable part: uncompressed PLY as the source and interchange format, SOG and Streamed SOG as quantised web-delivery formats with published specifications, Niantic's SPZ as a compressed single file, and binary glTF through KHR_gaussian_splatting, which Khronos has ratified, though the compression layer beneath it is contested, with three rival compression extensions open as pull requests against the specification and none merged. The strongest finding is the gap between the research and the wire: three separate well-cited lines of four-dimensional work model time inside the representation, through predicted per-frame deformation, through primitives that are genuinely four-dimensional, and through temporal opacity with per-primitive motion, and not one shipping format has a time axis. What ships instead is a numbered run of complete still frames played back like a flipbook, at whatever frame rate the playing script is set to, with the reference implementation of the best-known four-dimensional paper exporting exactly that; the maintainer of the main open editor has published the design for a proper four-dimensional format and its runtime encoding is still marked to be done. The second finding is that the family disagrees with itself about the coordinate frame, right up, back in SPZ against right, down, front in typical PLY and left, up, front in glTF, and an unstated frame is written through unconverted, so a file that survives a round trip can still come back mirrored. The third is what is entirely missing: no format carries a licence, an authorship record or a signature, which is a strange thing for a representation whose whole purpose is photographing real places and the people in them, and none carries units, so nothing states whether a captured room is two metres across or two hundred. Two traps for anyone planning to build on this. The reference implementation from Inria and the Max Planck Institute is licensed for research and evaluation only, not for commercial use, so several published results cannot legally be shipped as they stand, and the permissively licensed reimplementations must be checked one by one. And MPEG has started coding this representation inside its point-cloud standards, with a Gaussian splat profile amendment to video-based point cloud compression already at committee draft stage, which means a second, unrelated family of splat containers is arriving from a different direction.

subjects.name: Dynamic and four-dimensional Gaussian splat implementations
subjects.summary: This record covers the dynamic and four-dimensional splat research beyond the base technique row: the reference implementations that reconstruct a moving scene, the 2026 work on compressing and streaming one, and the commercial service that sells the result as volumetric video. The methods disagree about where time lives. Shape of Motion reconstructs a moving scene from a single ordinary video by learning a small set of shared motion bases; 4D-Rotor Gaussians make the primitive itself four-dimensional with a rotor-based rotation; MoSca fits a deformable scaffold to casual video; and the newest work treats a moving scene as a bitstream to be pruned, quantised and layered. All of it is research code with a research licence or none at all, most of it needs CUDA, and none of it writes a format any other implementation reads. The 2026 streaming papers state the interoperability problem in the plainest words this map has found anywhere: a four-dimensional model is a monolithic bitstream that a client must download in full before a single frame can be drawn, with first-frame waits measured in tens to hundreds of seconds on a mobile link. The one production pipeline in the family, Gracia, sells processed volumetric video delivered through its own engine kits and ships either a proprietary container or a numbered sequence of PLY files — which is exactly the flipbook the base technique row already describes, five hundred papers later.

subjects.name: Splat-to-avatar research families
subjects.summary: This record covers the research families that turn a capture of a person into an avatar you can drive. They all reach the same shape: a parametric human model supplies the motion, and Gaussian splats supply the look. GaussianAvatars rigs each splat to a triangle of a morphable face model with a local frame and a displacement; SplattingAvatar embeds splats on a triangle mesh by barycentric coordinates and walks them across it during optimisation, which it says makes the result compatible with skeletal animation, blend shapes and mesh editing; ExAvatar drives a whole body from a phone video through the SMPL-X model of body, hands and face; Gaussian Head Avatar drives dynamic Gaussians from expression coefficients on a studio multi-camera dataset; Meta's Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars add learned radiance transfer so the face can be relit in real time on a tethered headset; and the 2026 work makes an avatar from a single photograph. For a standards audience the conclusion is uncomfortable. This is the most advanced avatar work in existence and none of it reaches an avatar format: no VRM, no glTF with skinning, no named skeleton, no named expressions. The 'rig' is the parameter vector of a body model that has to be licensed separately for research use, and the deliverable is a checkpoint. On top of that the two best-known implementations carry a non-commercial research licence and no licence at all respectively, so even the code cannot ship.

subjects.name: Brush
subjects.summary: Brush is a Gaussian splat reconstruction engine written in Rust on the Burn machine-learning framework, licensed Apache-2.0, and it is the one trainer in this group that actually runs where the pictures are taken: the same code trains on Windows, macOS and Linux, on AMD, Intel and NVIDIA cards, on an Android phone, and inside a browser tab, because it targets WebGPU rather than CUDA. It takes a COLMAP or Nerfstudio dataset in and writes a splat PLY out, reads back both plain and SuperSplat-compressed PLY, streams a splat from a web address while it loads, and can bake several decimated levels of one scene as separate files. For a standards audience the interesting parts are at the edges. Time exists only as playback: a folder or zip of numbered PLY files, or a private 'PLY with delta frames' variant written for two research projects, neither of which is a published format. The coordinate frame is the input's frame and nothing in the exported file says which frame that is, a point the release notes state plainly. There is no scale, no licence field, no authorship record and no mesh: what comes out is a cloud of Gaussians and nothing else, so every question about rights, units and provenance is left to whatever carries the file. The project is a fork of a Google Research repository and says in its own README that it is not an official Google product.

subjects.name: Jawset Postshot
subjects.summary: Jawset Postshot is the desktop counterweight in this lane: a free-to-download Windows application that needs an NVIDIA card, keeps every image and every training step on the operator's own machine, and covers the whole path from a folder of photographs or a video to a trained radiance field that can be cropped, aligned, exported and dropped into Unreal Engine. It is scored here because it shows what the phone tools give up. It solves camera poses itself or imports them from COLMAP, Bundler or RealityScan; it reads professional image formats including raw and high-dynamic-range video, tracks the colour space through training and records it in the file; it will align a scene to a printed marker of a stated physical size, which is the only real-world scale mechanism found anywhere in this lane; and it writes its own non-standard metadata into the PLY header — colour space, anti-aliasing mode and world origin — because no splat format has anywhere to put them. Its export list is three items: a self-contained web page, lossless PLY, and SPZ with a version choice, and the reason given for keeping the older SPZ version is the honest state of splat interoperability — some third-party software does not read version 4 yet. There is no mesh, no time axis, no macOS or Linux build, and no statement of rights or authorship in anything it writes.

subjects.name: KIRI Engine
subjects.summary: KIRI Engine is a phone and web scanner from KIRI Innovation with a free tier, and it is the most open of the consumer capture products: alongside the closed application sits a set of separately licensed open-source pieces — a Blender add-on for importing, editing, animating and exporting splats, an After Effects plug-in, a desktop tool for preparing images and 360 footage, and, most interesting to a standards audience, colmap4d, a frozen version 1.0 specification with a conformance suite that adds a timestamp to every image and every point of a COLMAP model. It captures four ways — photogrammetry, lidar, a neural method for shiny and featureless objects, and Gaussian splatting — and it exports more than anything else in this lane: OBJ, STL, FBX, glTF, GLB, USDZ, PLY and XYZ. Two things make it matter here. Its splat captures come with a mesh, and that mesh then reaches the product's mesh features, including automatic skeleton generation, which is the only path in this whole map from a phone capture of a real thing to something with bones in it. And its open-source work is where the time problem is being attacked in the open, by a specification with golden test fixtures rather than by a private file variant. What it does not do is carry rights, authorship or any statement of scale in what it writes, and its splat editing and rigging live inside the service rather than in any format a second implementation could read.

subjects.name: Meta Horizon Hyperscape Capture
subjects.summary: Meta Horizon Hyperscape Capture is Meta's own answer to phone scanning, done with a headset: a Quest 3 or 3S user walks a room, the images and headset poses go to Meta's servers, and a Gaussian splat replica comes back, taking up to eight hours to process. It is scored here with the other capture product on the same platform — the experimental Splat interface in Meta's Spatial development kit, which loads splats on the same headsets from SPZ files — because together they show Meta's position clearly: the consumer capture path is closed and the developer path is open to a format somebody else published. Hyperscape shed features in 2026 rather than gaining them. Sharing a capture, inviting people into it and being in one together were all withdrawn on 12 May 2026; the worlds moved out of Horizon Worlds and are now view-only in the capture application itself, rendered on the headset instead of streamed from a server, and the separate preview application is gone. There is no export of any kind, no format, no interface for programs and no documented developer route into a Hyperscape capture: what you scan stays inside Meta's product on the headset that scanned it. The rules around capture, on the other hand, are the most explicit of any subject in this lane — a minimum room size, no people or pets, permission for the space, a code of conduct, a reporting tool, and a plain statement that the images go to Meta and may be used to improve Meta's products.

subjects.name: NVIDIA Omniverse NuRec and 3DGRUT
subjects.summary: NVIDIA Omniverse NuRec is the company's neural reconstruction and rendering stack for physical-AI simulation, and it is scored here together with 3DGRUT, the Apache-2.0 research code that trains the scenes and exports them. Real camera and lidar recordings go in through NCore, NVIDIA's documented multi-sensor data specification with its own pose graph, metric conventions and converters for the public driving datasets; a reconstruction comes out as a USD package that separates the static background from moving objects, carries a driveable road map, rig trajectories and the trained checkpoint, and is rendered by gsplat inside Isaac Sim or another simulator. Two things put this subject at the centre of the capture question for a standards group. First, splats have reached OpenUSD as a schema rather than as a private payload: Omniverse publishes these environments as USD stages using ParticleField geometry that the renderer draws natively alongside ordinary polygons, and NVIDIA is deprecating its own custom NuRec package in favour of that standard schema. Second, this is the only capture subject scored anywhere on the map that treats time as first-class — moving objects are separated into their own layers with tracks and trajectories — because the customer is a robot that has to drive through the scene. Everything here needs NVIDIA hardware, and much of it needs a container from NVIDIA's own registry; nothing here runs on a phone.

subjects.name: Nerfstudio and gsplat
subjects.summary: Nerfstudio is the Apache-2.0 research framework that made radiance-field training approachable, and gsplat is the splat rasteriser that grew out of it and is now the busier of the two. They are scored as one subject because that is how people use them: gsplat provides the rendering kernels, Nerfstudio's splatfacto method provides the training loop, the data ingestion and the viewer. The pair reaches further into ordinary content pipelines than any other free tool here — it ingests captures from Polycam, KIRI Engine, Record3D, Spectacular AI, Metashape, RealityCapture, drone mapping and Aria glasses, it runs COLMAP itself when there are only photographs, and for radiance fields it exports textured meshes and point clouds, not just splats. Two facts a standards audience should hold together. The first is a split in liveness: gsplat has shipped through 2026, taking NVIDIA's 3DGUT, lidar rasterisation, new sensor models and NCore capture support, while the Nerfstudio repository's own main branch has had no commit since 29 July 2025 and its last tagged release is from November 2024, so the documentation a newcomer reads is older than the library it describes. The second is that everything here needs CUDA: this is the group's most capable free trainer and it cannot run on a phone, in a browser, or on any machine without an NVIDIA card. What it writes is a PLY, or a private directory of PNG images when compression is used, and its default world-space normalisation throws away real scale unless the operator turns it off.

subjects.name: OpenSplat
subjects.summary: OpenSplat is a free C++ implementation of three-dimensional Gaussian splat training, licensed under the GNU Affero General Public Licence version 3, now developed inside the WebODM drone-mapping ecosystem. It is the plainest tool in this group: a command that takes a reconstruction someone else solved, in ODX, OpenSfM, COLMAP, OpenMVG or Nerfstudio project form, and trains a splat from it on an NVIDIA, AMD or Apple graphics card, or on the processor alone at roughly a hundredth of the speed. Two things make it matter to a standards group. First, it writes four different splat containers from one training run — plain PLY, the compact .splat, Niantic's SPZ and Spark's .RAD level-of-detail format — which makes it a useful witness to how unsettled that layer is, and its .RAD writer is a port of another project's Rust tool rather than an implementation of a published specification. Second, it is the only tool scored here that carries a real coordinate reference system through training: because its inputs come from mapping pipelines, it keeps the input translation and scale by default and offers a switch to centre the result for viewers that cannot cope. What it does not do is run on a phone, solve its own camera poses, produce a mesh, or write a single field about licence, authorship or units into any of its four outputs.

subjects.name: Polycam
subjects.summary: Polycam is a free phone scanner with a paid professional service around it, and in 2026 its centre of gravity has moved: the product describes itself first as a way of turning one phone scan into the documents a building job runs on — floor plans, as-builts, measurements, claim files — and second as a 3D capture tool. That reframing is the interesting part for this map, because it drags real-world units, measurement tolerance and computer-aided-design formats into a lane where almost nothing else has them. It captures with lidar, with photogrammetry, with Gaussian splats from photographs or video, with drone imagery and with 360 imagery, on iOS, Android, the web and Apple's headset. It exports more conventional formats than any other tool scored here — OBJ, DAE, FBX, STL, DXF, PLY and an insurance estimating format — and it will hand you a mesh derived from any splat, which is a bridge from captured content back to ordinary geometry that most of its peers do not offer. Against that, its splat interchange story is thin and it says so itself: support for splats in other software is a work in progress. Nothing it writes carries a licence, an author or a signature; there is no time axis anywhere; and the programmatic route out of the library — list captures, fetch metadata, export OBJ, glTF or LAS — is an enterprise add-on rather than part of the product everyone can use.

subjects.name: Scaniverse
subjects.summary: Scaniverse is Niantic Spatial's phone scanner, free on iOS and Android and now paired with a cloud service and a web application. It is the most complete free path from a phone in a pocket to a splat that other tools can read, and in 2026 it is two products under one name: 'Scaniverse Classic', which scans, trains and exports entirely on the device with no account needed for the scanning itself, and the new Scaniverse, where scans upload to Niantic Spatial's servers, several people's scans of one site are combined, and the result comes back as a Gaussian splat, a mesh, or a positioning map for the company's visual positioning service. It matters to this map for three reasons. It writes SPZ, the openly licensed splat container the rest of the industry has adopted, whose fourth version arrived in May 2026 with a plaintext header, parallel compression streams and a vendor extension chain — the only splat format scored here with an extension mechanism at all. It exports a USDZ package that carries a splat and an automatically aligned mesh together, aimed at robot simulation, which is the clearest example anywhere in this map of captured content reaching a conventional scene container without being thrown away. And it georeferences: a capture can be dragged onto a map until it sits where it really is, then serve as a positioning map. What it does not do is time — nothing here captures or carries a moving scene — and nothing it writes states a licence or an author.

subjects.name: Babylon.js
subjects.summary: Babylon.js is an open-source web rendering engine and application framework from Microsoft and community contributors, shipping as one core package plus official sibling packages for asset loading, asset saving, user interface, add-ons and editors; the newest release when this was written is 9.22.1, published 2026-08-20. It is far more than a renderer: it covers the scene graph, animation, skinning, morph targets, instancing, glTF import and export with a very wide extension set, Gaussian splat rendering, a node-based material system, a node-based frame graph, and a full immersive session stack on the WebXR Device API with controller, hand, eye and body tracking. Physics is not in the engine at all. Every physics row below is delivered by a plug-in wrapping an outside engine: Havok is the only one on the current second-generation physics interface, and Ammo.js on the older interface is the only one that does soft bodies and cloth. It does no networking, no shared state, no identity and no persistence beyond writing a file on the client, so a multi-user world built on it must get all of that from somewhere else. Three traps for a standards audience: the scene is left-handed and Y-up by default, so right-handed glTF content is imported under a wrapper node carrying a negative Z scale unless the application opts into a right-handed scene; the WebGPU engine, which the project itself calls complete, still has no multiview, so immersive sessions in practice run on WebGL; and the loaders reach out to Babylon's own content network by default to fetch the Draco, meshopt, KTX2 and Basis decoders, which the project's own documentation warns against in production. Levels below read 'native' for anything shipped and maintained by the Babylon.js project itself, with the package named in the note, and 'via-extension' for anything that needs software from outside the project.

subjects.name: CesiumJS
subjects.summary: CesiumJS is an open source JavaScript library for drawing a whole-Earth globe and streaming very large geographic three-dimensional data into a web browser. Its strength is the geospatial half of the map: everything sits on the World Geodetic System 1984 ellipsoid in Earth-centred fixed coordinates, terrain and imagery and city-scale models stream by tile, and the clock is built on International Atomic Time with a leap second table rather than on browser time. Cesium created the 3D Tiles format, later approved by the Open Geospatial Consortium as a community standard, and CesiumJS is its reference implementation; it also reads glTF, the Indexed 3D Scene Layer format, and its own time-aware scene language, and it now streams captured scenes as Gaussian splats through the Khronos splatting extensions. It leaves almost everything a shared virtual world needs to others: the library contains no physics, no audio of any kind, no avatar or skeleton standard, and no multi-user networking. Two traps for a standards audience: CesiumJS has a complete position-and-orientation-on-Earth model of its own but does not read or write the Open Geospatial Consortium GeoPose encoding, which appears nowhere in the source tree; and its stereoscopic viewing mode predates the WebXR Device API and does not use it, so CesiumJS cannot drive a headset through the standard web path. All findings below were checked against the library source at version 1.144.0.

subjects.name: PlayCanvas
subjects.summary: PlayCanvas is two things under one name: an open-source runtime released under the MIT licence, and a hosted editor and publishing service at playcanvas.com. The runtime is a mature real-time renderer on WebGL 2 and WebGPU, with an entity-and-component scene model, glTF 2.0 reading and writing, animation state graphs, positioned sound, WebXR sessions, and unusually deep support for Gaussian splats including level-of-detail streaming. Physics is not in the runtime: rigid bodies, collision shapes, joints and trigger volumes ship as components that stay inert until the application separately loads ammo.js, a WebAssembly port of Bullet. The runtime carries no networking, no identity, no persistence and no avatar model at all, and PlayCanvas documents multi-user work only as tutorials that wire a scene to a third-party server such as Socket.io, Colyseus or Photon. The first trap for a standards audience is the product split: reading FBX or COLLADA, baking font atlases, compressing textures, resolving template overrides and producing a runnable package are all hosted-editor jobs done on PlayCanvas servers, and none of them exist in the open-source runtime. The second trap is that several load-bearing conventions, including right-handed axes with Y up, column-major matrices and one unit to the metre, are stated in source comments or a single documentation page rather than specified anywhere normative.

subjects.name: Three.js
subjects.summary: Three.js is an open source JavaScript library for drawing three-dimensional scenes in a web browser. Its core covers drawing and scene structure: a scene tree, cameras, materials, lights and shadows, skinning, morph targets, instancing, keyframe animation, positioned sound through the browser's own audio engine, and an immersive session manager that drives WebXR. Almost everything else people associate with the library sits in the addons folder of the same repository as optional modules rather than in the core build: every file format reader and writer including glTF, USD and FBX, all post-processing on the WebGL path, the camera controls, and thin wrappers around three outside physics engines that are fetched from a content delivery network at run time. There is no networking of any kind, no avatar format or skeleton agreement, no identity, rights or provenance model, and no geospatial frame. Two traps for a standards audience: the WebGL renderer is still the default import and the WebGPU renderer is a separate entry point, and a growing set of newer features (Gaussian splats, MaterialX materials) runs only on the WebGPU path. A third: the whole Gaussian splat stack is on the development branch and is in no tagged release up to r185, so a claim that Three.js renders splats is true of the branch and not of the shipped library.

subjects.name: NVIDIA Cosmos
subjects.summary: NVIDIA Cosmos is a family of world models for what NVIDIA calls physical AI: robots, vehicles and machines that act in the real world. The current family, Cosmos 3, was published on 31 May 2026 under the Linux Foundation's OpenMDW-1.1 licence, with open weights in three sizes and a training and serving framework beside them. It has two faces. One reads pictures and video and writes text, answering questions about what is happening, when it happened and where in the frame it is. The other generates: given a text prompt, a starting image, a video or a stream of actions, it produces images, video, sound muxed into the video, and action trajectories for a named robot or vehicle, including the future a given action would bring about and the actions that would bring about a given future.
