Scored against this map it is almost entirely out of scope, and that is the finding rather than a gap in the research: sixty-four of the eighty-nine rows describe machinery Cosmos does not have, because it has no scene, no objects, no transforms, no materials, no lights and no physics engine, and its own limitation notice says so, stating that the model lacks an explicit physics simulator and that geometry, object permanence and contact dynamics are only approximated. What it does have that this map can see is narrow and worth naming: a camera it can be driven by and can estimate, in nine numbers a frame; a time-sampled action record; scene text as a measured concern; and a guardrail on generation. Four things a standards audience should carry away. The only structured description of a scene in the whole platform is the JSON prompt handed to the generator, and every field in it is prose, so the interchange artefact of a world model is a paragraph in slots. The action trajectory, which is the one numeric record Cosmos both reads and writes, cannot be read by anything else: its columns mean whatever the named embodiment says they mean, its values are normalised by figures taken from the training set, and decoding them needs a projection matrix that lives inside the model. Nothing marks a Cosmos output as generated, though a safety classifier and a face blur do run over the frames. And nothing anywhere expresses a position on the Earth, in a platform trained on ten thousand hours of driving. Two traps for anyone planning on this. The autoencoder in the generation path is not NVIDIA's: it is taken from the Wan2.2 model, published by Wan-AI under Apache 2.0, and kept frozen, so a separately owned component sits inside what an OpenMDW notice appears to cover. And the platform's own publications already contradict each other: the documentation site still gives Apache 2.0 and the NVIDIA Open Model License where the repository, the model card and the technical report all give OpenMDW-1.1, and says the guardrail cannot be disabled where the shipped code documents four ways to disable it.

subjects.name: Tencent Hunyuan World 2.0
subjects.summary: Tencent's HY-World 2.0, which the map lists as Hunyuan World 2.0, is a model that turns a sentence, a photograph, a set of photographs or a video into a three-dimensional place, and its whole argument is that the place should be a file rather than a film: where a video world model draws the next frame forever, this one runs once and hands you Gaussian splats, a fused mesh and a point cloud that an ordinary engine can open. Two halves sit in one repository. Reconstruction takes pictures and returns depth, surface normals, camera poses, intrinsics, points and splats in a single pass, and will take known cameras or depth as a prior. Generation makes a 360-degree panorama, parses it into a mesh and a navigation mesh, has a vision-language model plan collision-free camera routes through it, generates the views those routes would see, and fits a splat scene to the result. It is genuinely open in the sense that weights, code and a detailed report are published, and genuinely not open source: the licence excludes the European Union, the United Kingdom and South Korea, forbids using the outputs to improve any other model, and requires a separate grant above a million monthly users. For a standards audience the important part is what does not come out. Everything it writes is somebody else's format used as-is — splat and mesh PLY, the compressed SPZ form, a COLMAP model, a camera JSON — with no scene graph, no object identity, no units, no licence field, no signature and no statement that the place was manufactured rather than photographed. There is no specification of the output and no conformance test, and the documentation chapter for the generation pipeline reads coming soon. Two claims in the technical report describe a rendering platform called WorldLens, with image-based lighting, collision and character control; it is not in the repository or the open-source plan, so the interactive, lit, walkable world the report shows cannot be reproduced from the release, and the rows here are scored on what was published.

subjects.name: World Labs Marble
subjects.summary: Marble is World Labs' hosted generative world model and the product built on it: give it a sentence, one or several photographs, a 360 panorama, a short video or a coarse block-out you draw in its own modelling tool, and about five minutes later you get back a three-dimensional place you can walk around in a browser. The place is stored as several million three-dimensional Gaussian splats, which the vendor calls its highest-fidelity form, and it can also be handed over as a coarse mesh for physics, as two higher-quality meshes for drawing, as a panorama, or as a recorded video. It can be edited by describing the change, grown past its original edges, varied by changing a seed, and several worlds can be placed beside one another into a larger one. Everything else a shared world needs is absent by design: no session, no participants, no identity, no rules, no sound and no position on the Earth, which is why fifty-eight of the eighty-nine rows here are honestly out of scope. Two traps matter for a standards audience. The first is that Marble writes an open splat format in a coordinate frame that format does not expect, corrects for it in its own viewer, and describes the frame three different ways across three of its own pages - so a conforming reader gets an upside-down world. The second is that the words reconstruct, generate and simulate are used together in the vendor's own framing, while what actually ships simulates nothing: it produces a static asset for someone else's engine to run, and the vendor's own writing places interactivity in the future.

tooltips.render.raster: This row asks whether a subject turns scene geometry into pixels itself: the loop that draws triangles onto the display, and the order its passes run in. Built in means the subject owns that loop. Thirteen do, two are partial, and seven score out of scope and are hidden, because a delivery format says what to draw, not how a frame is assembled. Most of these pipelines are engine-private, so a filled cell is not a shared pass structure.
tooltips.render.gpu-api: This row records which driver-level graphics interface a renderer speaks: Vulkan, Metal, Direct3D or WebGPU. Built in means the choice sits in the subject's own core. Eleven score that way, one reaches it only through an extension, two are partial and two are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. Read it beside the immersive session row: both read supported and still do not compose, so a filled row is never proof that two systems will work together.
tooltips.render.material: This row is the numbers a surface carries so light behaves the same on it in two renderers: base colour, metal, roughness. Built in means the subject defines that surface model itself. Twelve do, one reaches it through an extension, one is partial, three are out of scope and hidden, and one conflicts. Horizon Worlds reads a surface's shading model out of the spelling of the material's name, so a material cannot survive the trip in either direction.
tooltips.render.lighting: This row covers shadows, bounced light and probes, baked ahead of time or worked out live. Nine subjects have a light model built in, seven are partial, one is out of scope and hidden, and Horizon Worlds conflicts by baking light into mesh vertex colours. One reaches it only through an extension: the common transfer format has ratified punctual lights and no shadows, probes or baked light, while the older ratified scene standard gives the equations in its core. Check the older standard first.
tooltips.render.post: Post-processing is what happens after the main draw: bloom, tone mapping, anti-aliasing. Seven subjects have it built in, two reach it only through separate packages, one is partial, one is absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Read supported carefully here: on this row it often means an add-on rather than engine core, and Resonite's effects are a viewer setting that no scene can carry with it.
tooltips.render.lod: This row is choosing how much detail to draw, and what to send down the wire first. Six subjects have both halves built in, one reaches it through a single-vendor extension, ten are partial, and three are out of scope and hidden. Partial here almost always means detail selection works and send order does not. It is the one rendering row settled at connection time, because once geometry streams the sender and the receiver have to agree on the order.
tooltips.render.splat: This row draws a captured place as many soft blobs instead of triangles. Four subjects have it built in, one reaches it through addons, two are partial, seven are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones are engines and platforms that could carry such a renderer and ship none. The extension that would move splats between tools is at release candidate stage, announced 2026-02-03 and not ratified, and it says how to store splats, not how to draw them.
tooltips.render.volumetric: This row covers point clouds, voxels and volumetric video rather than surfaces. Two subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a plug-in, ten are partial, two are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. Partial nearly always means the same thing here: a static point cloud can be shown, while volumetric video is missing and often the voxel path too. Do not read a partial cell as support for captured moving volume.
tooltips.render.text: This row is words that stay legible inside a scene, with real fonts and layout. Nine subjects have it built in, two reach it through addons, three are partial, one is absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. It matters because a shared world that cannot draw the same label twice cannot carry a sign, a menu or a name badge across a boundary. One limit: the TeleportXR claim on this row rests on local files and has no public source yet.
tooltips.render.camera: This row is how a viewpoint is defined, attached to something, and moved between. Fourteen subjects have it built in, eight are partial, and one is out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. One caution: the transfer formats and the immersive runtimes each define a camera and they are not the same object. A file's camera carries projection settings, while a runtime hands the application a viewer pose and one projection per view every frame.
tooltips.scene.graph: The scene graph is the tree that says what exists, what it hangs off, and where it sits. Seventeen subjects have one built in, one is partial, one conflicts, and four are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. Keep the qualifier: in the major engines the tree is the engine's own and no outside tool reads it, yet three ratified standards define one natively. The RP1 and TeleportXR claims here rest on local files with no public source.
tooltips.scene.transform: This row is handedness, which axis points up, and the order transforms multiply in. Twelve subjects settle it in their core, eight are partial, one is absent, and four conflict. This is where silent failure lives. The draft avatar format writes its matrices the other way round from the common transfer format, and one platform is left-handed with Y up and positive Z forward, so a converter that copies the numbers straight across loads with no error and places the thing wrongly. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.scene.container: This row is the single file you hand somebody: the binary transfer file, the zipped scene package, the platform bundle. Twelve subjects have one built in, two reach it through an extension, seven are partial, six are out of scope and hidden, and four conflict. Horizon Worlds, Roblox and VRChat compile an upload into a private bundle nobody else can open, and TeleportXR states it has no file format at all. The RP1 claim rests on local files with no public source.
tooltips.scene.geometry: This row is how a mesh is written down and squeezed: vertex data, index data, compression. Nine subjects have it built in, ten are partial, one is absent, three are out of scope and hidden, and one conflicts. Partial usually means meshes move while the compressed forms do not. The conflict is Resonite: every mesh that enters is converted to its own representation and the link to the source file is dropped, so it cannot give the file back. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.scene.texture: This row is the image formats and compressed forms a target device can actually decode. Eleven subjects have it built in, nine are partial, and two are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. The thing to notice is that this is decided by the device rather than by a standard: one asset usually has to carry two or three compressed forms to reach a phone, a desktop and a headset. TeleportXR's claim here has no public source.
tooltips.scene.material-x: Material exchange is handing a material from one renderer to another without the surface changing. Two subjects have it built in, one through an addon, seven partial, six absent, two conflicting, three out of scope and hidden. The absent ones could carry a neutral material description and none does. The best case is here: the older ratified scene standard says its material is deliberately consistent with the common transfer format's, so converting either way is equivalent, unlike the lossy partial scores. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.scene.animation: This row is keyframes and clips: what moves, when, and how it is worked out between keys. Thirteen subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a separate file, four are partial, one is absent, one conflicts, and three are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. Say the limit in the format's own words: glTF 2.0 only supports animating node transforms and morph target weights. A ratified extension lifts that; the core does not. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.scene.skeleton: This row is the bone list and its parentage, so a body authored once moves correctly somewhere else. Thirteen subjects have it built in, three are partial, two are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. A ratified international standard already binds a humanoid skeleton in as nodes, with joints, segments, attachment sites and displacers, and the newer formats passed it over. The gap here is adoption, not capability. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.scene.morph: This row is moving vertices to change a shape, the way a face smiles without new bones. Nine subjects have it built in, six are partial, two are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. Partial here usually means the shapes work inside the system and cannot be written back out. One conversion trap: in the draft avatar format a shape is a whole replacement mesh with matching topology, not the per-vertex offsets the common transfer format uses, so the two do not copy across.
tooltips.scene.instancing: Instancing is drawing one tree ten thousand times without carrying ten thousand copies of it. Fourteen subjects have it built in, two reach it through an extension, two are partial, and two are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. It belongs on an interoperability map because instancing is where a scene's size stops being a question about file size and becomes a question about the wire format: the receiver has to be told these are copies.
tooltips.scene.compose: This row is building one scene by referencing and overriding parts of other files. Three subjects have it built in, two reach it through a plug-in, twelve are partial, three are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. Partial almost always means referencing works and ordered override does not. The scene description core, version 1.0.1 dated 2025-12-12, is the one thing that standardises this machinery, and the same document excludes geometry, materials and physics by name. The RP1 claim has no public source.
tooltips.scene.units: This row is agreeing that one unit means one metre, so an imported chair arrives chair-sized. Twelve subjects settle it, six are partial, three are absent, one is out of scope and hidden, and three conflict: Roblox, whose unit is 28 centimetres and which converts nothing, plus the RP1 fabric and Web of Worlds, which declare no unit. The ratified scene description core defines no unit of length and no up axis, both appearing only in example code, so adopting it does not give you scale agreement.
tooltips.scene.licence: This row is the line inside a file saying what a recipient may do with it. One subject has it built in: VRM, which requires a name, an author and a licence link, plus eleven machine-readable permission settings. Three reach it through an extension, four are partial, nine absent, one conflicting, four out of scope and hidden. Licence metadata is covered, with no second built-in answer to point at; rights enforcement, further down the map, is reached by nobody. Collapsing the two is the error.
tooltips.scene.provenance: A signed record that travels with an asset, saying who made it and what was done to it. Two subjects have it built in, five are partial, fourteen are absent, one conflicts, and three are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones record an author as plain text and sign nothing. The gap is narrow and fillable: the provenance specification lists no three-dimensional format, so a model can only be covered by a separate file with nothing keeping the two together. RP1's claim has no public source.
tooltips.avatar.body: This row is the portable description of an avatar's mesh and look, so the same person shows up recognisably elsewhere. Start with the three conflicts: Horizon Worlds, Resonite and VRChat each take a body in and let none out. Four subjects have it built in, three reach it through an extension, three are partial, seven are absent, and six are out of scope and hidden. The draft international standard here is not the first attempt: the same committee published one in 2016 to migrate a virtual object between virtual worlds.
tooltips.avatar.skeleton: This row is an agreed bone list and parentage, so animation transfers: the widely used open avatar format names 55 human bones, 15 of them required, each with a fixed parent. Four subjects have it built in, ten are partial, six are absent, and two are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones carry bones with no agreed names. A ratified international standard already binds a humanoid skeleton, while the common transfer format has no avatar extension at any registry stage, so do not cite one.
tooltips.avatar.expression: This row is named expressions and mouth shapes, happy and angry and the mouth positions for speech, that survive a move between worlds. One subject has it built in: VRM, with eighteen preset names. Six are partial, seven absent, one conflicts, and two are out of scope and hidden. It is one of the nine thin rows, and VRM is the only answer to point at. Resonite's mouth shapes match an outside vendor's published fifteen-entry list index for index, while its ninety expression names are its own.
tooltips.avatar.retarget: Retargeting is playing a walk cycle authored for one body on a body with different proportions. Six subjects have it built in, two reach it through addons, one is partial, four are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Every built-in answer works only inside its own runtime. The draft avatar format solves less than it appears to: it maps parameter to parameter between tracking frameworks, with the mapping authored into the file in advance, not motion between differently proportioned bodies.
tooltips.avatar.wearable: This row is a hat, a badge or a tool that stays attached in the right place after the avatar moves worlds. One subject has it built in: Roblox, which publishes its attachment point names and its layered clothing cages. Eight are partial, six are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. It is one of the nine thin rows, and one of five where a closed platform is the only built-in answer, so there is no open answer to point an implementer at.
tooltips.avatar.lod: This row is a cheaper version of an avatar for a crowd of two hundred, or for a weak phone. Four subjects have it built in, three are partial, five are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Partial means general mesh reduction exists with nothing avatar-aware on top. It is settled at connection time because the receiving world, not the author, decides how much avatar it can afford, and none of the reduced forms built so far can be exported.
tooltips.avatar.identity: State the interest first: one of the two answers here is the co-chair's own draft, the Universal Manifest. The row asks whether the avatar in front of you can be proved to belong to the person claiming it. Two subjects have it built in, that draft and Roblox; five are partial and three absent. Nine score out of scope and are hidden, because a drawing library or a device interface holds no notion of a person, so the low count is a scoping result. That claim has no public source.
tooltips.physics.rigid: Rigid bodies are mass, velocity and the objects that move by rule rather than by script. Seven subjects have them built in, three reach them through a plug-in, one is partial, six are absent, and six are out of scope and hidden, because a delivery format never says how anything moves. A ratified international standard has defined rigid bodies since its 2008 edition and still does in the current fourth edition of December 2023, though only in its fullest profile. The common transfer format has nothing ratified.
tooltips.physics.collision: Collision shapes are the invisible shapes used for contact tests, and they are not the shapes you see. Eight subjects have them built in, three reach them through a plug-in, two are partial, two are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. They are kept separate because testing against a visible mesh is too expensive, so every engine carries a second, cruder body. Nothing carries that second body between engines: the collision extension for the common transfer format is still a review draft.
tooltips.physics.joint: Joints and constraints are the hinges, sliders and other links that hold two bodies together. Five subjects have them built in, two reach them through a plug-in, one is partial, three are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Every built-in answer is engine-private and none travels. The older ratified scene standard names six joint types: ball, single-axis hinge, double-axis hinge, motor, slider and universal. The extension name people cite for the common transfer format is not in its registry at all.
tooltips.physics.material: Physics materials are friction and bounce: whether a box slides or grips, whether a ball comes back. Four subjects have them built in, one reaches them through a plug-in, two are partial, one is absent, two conflict, and five are out of scope and hidden. Roblox's friction runs 0 to 2 rather than 0 to 1 and combines two surfaces by a pairwise weighted average rather than by multiply, minimum or maximum, so imported friction values do not reproduce the same contact. Horizon Worlds offers named presets only.
tooltips.physics.determinism: Deterministic simulation is two machines running the same inputs and getting the same result. No subject reaches it natively. One gets there through an optional package, three are partial, six are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones are engines and platforms expected to publish a repeatability guarantee and none does; several state the opposite, naming one machine the owner and copying its answer. The honest description is covered only partially, which is weaker and different from empty.
tooltips.physics.soft: Soft bodies and cloth are anything that deforms rather than staying rigid: cloth, rope, hair. Two subjects have them built in, one reaches them through a plug-in, three are partial, five are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Partial usually means cloth only, and only on a character. Nothing standard exists because the result depends on the solver and on the size of the time step, so the same file gives different cloth in two runtimes.
tooltips.physics.trigger: A trigger volume is an invisible region that fires an event when something enters it: a doorway, a checkpoint. Nine subjects have it built in, two reach it through a plug-in, one is partial, three are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. It is the cheapest piece of interactivity on this map, and one of the nine is the older ratified scene standard, whose proximity sensor timestamps the moment of entry. The rest are runtimes, and none of their triggers travels in a file.
tooltips.audio.source: This row is a sound placed at a point in the scene that gets quieter and changes direction as you walk. Fifteen subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a single-vendor extension, three are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. This is the best-covered audio row on the map. The next four fall away quickly: spatialisation, rooms, occlusion and voice each have far fewer built-in answers.
tooltips.audio.spatial: This row is how a direction becomes something two ears can tell apart: head-related transfer functions, or ambisonics. Five subjects have it built in, two reach it through unratified single-vendor extensions, ten are partial, and five are out of scope and hidden. Partial usually means the browser or engine pans between channels and names no ear model. State the evidence limit before anyone asks: the immersive audio standard's normative text is sold rather than published, so all of its rows here sit at second-hand confidence.
tooltips.audio.room: Room acoustics is why a cathedral and a cupboard sound different: reverberation and early reflections. Six subjects have it built in, four are partial, four are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. Partial almost always means a hand-placed reverb zone rather than acoustics worked out from the geometry. There is a duplication cost worth naming: the immersive audio standard takes its own description of the room, separate from however the room is described for pictures, so one room gets described twice.
tooltips.audio.occlusion: Occlusion is a voice behind a closed door sounding muffled rather than clear. Three subjects have it built in, one is partial, nine are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones are engines and platforms with full positioned audio that never test what stands between source and listener; each expects the application to cast its own rays. The older ratified scene standard does not cover it either: the words occlusion and obstruction occur zero times in its sound clause.
tooltips.audio.stream: Audio streaming is getting sound to a thousand listeners without sending a thousand separate copies. Four subjects have it built in, eight are partial, two are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Partial nearly always means reading a long file off local disk, which is easy to mistake for delivery over a network. It is settled at connection time because the codec, the buffer and the fan-out are agreed when two systems connect. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.audio.voice: Voice transport is carrying a person's live voice from their microphone to everyone else's ears. Three subjects have it built in, two reach it through a hosted service, four are partial, four are absent, and five are out of scope and hidden. Partial usually means voice works and the transport is unpublished. Here is the gap beside an otherwise complete standard: the immersive audio standard can render a talker's voice into a scene once it arrives and defines nothing about carrying it. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.net.replication: This row is which parts of a world's state are sent to whom, how often, and in what shape. Seven subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a package, five are partial, three are absent, and nine are out of scope and hidden, because a file format has no second participant. A ratified international standard defines networked state sharing across host computers, bound to a long-established simulation protocol, and nothing else on this map has it. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.net.authority: Authority is the answer to a plain question: when two people grab the same cup, whose copy is right. Seven subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a package, two are partial, three are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Every built-in answer is a runtime; no standard on this map defines authority at all. It is the first thing any federation proposal has to answer. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.net.interest: Interest management is not telling a client about the room it is not in. Three subjects have it built in, five are partial, four are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Partial usually means the runtime hands the developer a visibility callback and no rule of its own. It decides cost rather than only correctness: it is what makes a thousand-person world affordable, and the platforms without it send every movement to everybody. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.net.prediction: Prediction and reconciliation is moving your own hand immediately, then quietly correcting when the server disagrees. Two subjects have it built in, two are partial, six are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Both built-in answers are runtimes and both are internal to their own engine, so there is nothing yet for a standard to profile. The absent ones take the opposite approach: smooth between the values that arrive rather than guess ahead and correct.
tooltips.net.transport: This row is the wire protocol itself: what a packet looks like and how a connection is set up. Three subjects have it built in, one through a package, six partial, four absent, one conflicting, and six out of scope and hidden, because a drawing library opens no socket. The recorded conflict is about publication, not capability: VRChat has a working transport and names no protocol, port, framing or handshake, which is why the row is second-hand. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.net.media: Media transport is carrying live video and sound alongside the world's state. Two subjects have it built in, two reach it through engine packages, five are partial, three are absent, and five are out of scope and hidden. This is the networking row with the most mature outside answer, the open real-time web transport, and the map mostly records it as an engine plug-in rather than as engine core. Partial usually means media moves one way only. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.net.session: Session establishment is the handshake that gets a person from a link into a running world, including proving who they are. Three subjects have it built in, two reach it through engine services, eight are partial, three are absent, and five are out of scope and hidden. Every built-in answer is single-operator. The identity specifications stop before the session and say so, though the sentence saying it sits under a line reading this section is non-normative. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.net.handoff: Disclose first: one of the two built-in answers is the draft of a body the owner co-chairs. This row is walking through a door in one world and arriving in another still holding what you were holding. Two are built in, five partial, seven absent, three conflicting, and seven out of scope and hidden, because a file format moves no people. Plain traversal is ratified; nothing ratified carries your state across. VRChat's own documentation says persistent data cannot be shared between different worlds.
tooltips.net.presence: Presence and roster is knowing who is online and where they are, across two operators who do not share a database. No subject reaches it natively. Two get there through engine back-end services, which are commercial products rather than standards; seven are partial, five are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. Partial always means the same thing here: a roster works inside one operator's own service and nothing crosses the boundary.
tooltips.net.address: This row is typing a name for a place and arriving at a joinable destination, the way a web address works. Four subjects reach it natively, seven are partial, six absent, two conflicting, five out of scope and hidden. The absent ones offer a host and port with no name. Say the careful version: no ratified standard from an accredited body does both halves, naming and resolving. A European survey of 912 standards and 354 technical reports found none. The RP1 and Web of Worlds claims have no public source.
tooltips.net.discovery: Discovery is finding a world, a node or a service you were never told about. Two subjects have it built in, one reaches it through an engine service, five are partial, eight are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones expect you to arrive already holding an address, which is what separates this row from addressing: addressing assumes you have the name. Both built-in answers find only their own operator's things.
tooltips.net.time: A clock and time model is two machines agreeing what happened first. One subject has it built in: Roblox, whose server time reads the same for every client. One reaches it through a package, ten are partial, five absent, three out of scope and hidden. Partial almost always means a clock that orders events on one machine only. It is one of the nine thin rows, and the one that took the count of capabilities only that closed platform answers from four to five. There is no second answer.
tooltips.identity.root: An identity root is the name a person or thing carries that its own holder controls, rather than one an account provider issues. Three subjects have it built in, two reach it through engine services, eleven are partial, and ten are out of scope and hidden, because a drawing library holds no notion of a person. The core identifier recommendation is dated 2022-07-19; its revision has sat at candidate stage since 2026-03-05. 267 methods are registered as of 2026-08-12, none standardised. The Universal Manifest claim has no public source.
tooltips.identity.credential: A credential format is how a signed statement one party makes about you is written down, checkable by a third party without asking the first. Two subjects have it built in, one through another body's assertion, three partial, nine absent, seven out of scope and hidden. The data model became a full recommendation on 2025-05-15, with companion recommendations the same day, and it does not require decentralised identifiers: those are one example among plain identifiers and web addresses. The Universal Manifest claim has no public source.
tooltips.identity.exchange: A credential exchange protocol is the back and forth in which one side asks for a credential and the other hands it over. One subject has it built in: Roblox, using ordinary authorization-code sign-in. Four are partial, eight absent, six out of scope and hidden. It is one of the nine thin rows with a closed platform as the only answer. No ratified recommendation defines the exchange; the one finished specification, dated 2025-07-09, is at another body, and the matching work is a working draft targeting 2028.
tooltips.identity.capability: Disclose the interest first: the only built-in answer here is the owner's own draft, the Universal Manifest, at version 0.4. The row is a permission a receiving world can read and act on. One is built in, one reaches it through an optional profile, nine partial, three absent, five out of scope and hidden. The slot exists and the vocabulary does not: the identifier standard defines capability invocation and delegation, and the credential model has a terms-of-use field. That claim has no public source and no second answer.
tooltips.identity.privacy: Disclose the interest first: the only built-in answer is the owner's own draft, the Universal Manifest. Selective disclosure is showing a bar you are over eighteen without showing it your birthday. One is built in, four are partial, seven absent, seven out of scope and hidden. The hard part is who chooses: the issuer must secure a credential with a mechanism supporting selective disclosure at the moment of issue, so a person cannot narrow one they already hold. That claim has no public source and no second answer.
tooltips.identity.social: This row is your friends list and your standing following you into a world your friends are not on. No subject reaches it natively. Two get there through engine back-end services, which are commercial products rather than standards; five are partial and seven are out of scope and hidden, because a drawing library models no relationships. With half the map scoped out, the row is thinly scored rather than thoroughly empty.
tooltips.identity.rights: Rights enforcement is a world refusing to copy a model because the licence that travelled with it said so. Nothing on this map reaches it: six subjects are partial, six are absent, one conflicts, and six are out of scope and hidden. It is one of only two capabilities that nothing reaches natively or through an extension. Under the looser reading, where partial counts, it is not empty at all. Keep the split: licence metadata is covered; acting on the licence is not.
tooltips.geo.pose: A geospatial pose says where a thing is on Earth and which way it faces, in a form two systems can exchange. Three subjects have it built in, two through unratified extensions, two partial, nine absent, one conflicting, seven out of scope and hidden, because a virtual world has no place on the Earth. Say the defect before somebody finds it: the ratified standard's tangent-point latitude rule reads minimum 90.0 degrees and maximum 90.0 degrees, the minus sign missing, so read literally it permits only the north pole.
tooltips.geo.crs: A coordinate reference system is the agreement about which frame a coordinate is measured in, before two of them are compared. Three subjects have it built in, two through a plug-in, two partial, seven absent, seven out of scope and hidden, because a virtual world has one frame of its own. The failure is real rather than pedantic: the flexible pose form names an outside authority and says interpreting it is out of scope, so two conforming systems can exchange a valid pose and still disagree about where it is.
tooltips.geo.anchor-local: A local anchor is putting a virtual chair on your actual floor and having it stay there while you walk around it. Three subjects have it built in, four reach it through extensions, three are partial, one is absent, and six are out of scope and hidden, because a fully virtual platform has no real room to anchor to. This row is well covered and the next one is not, and the difference is the whole problem: one device against many devices and many sessions.
tooltips.geo.anchor-shared: This row is two people in the same room seeing the same virtual chair in the same place, and it still being there tomorrow. No subject reaches it natively. One gets there through engine plug-ins, seven are partial, three are absent, and five are out of scope and hidden. Partial means the same thing almost every time: persistence across sessions is solved and sharing across devices is not. Every extension with sharing in its name is single-vendor and unratified.
tooltips.geo.vps: Visual positioning is working out exactly where a phone is by looking at what its camera sees. No subject reaches it natively. One gets there through a single-vendor unratified extension, five are absent, and eight are out of scope and hidden, because a fully virtual platform never takes camera imagery of the real world. Do not call this a thin cell: thin means exactly one subject claims it natively, and none does. The honest description is covered only partially.
tooltips.geo.tiles: This row is streaming a whole city of three-dimensional data by loading only the tiles you can see. Three subjects have it built in, three reach it through outside libraries, one is absent, and ten are out of scope and hidden, because an invented world has no such data. Note the standing: the tiled standard here is a Community Standard at the Open Geospatial Consortium, not an Implementation Standard, submitted by a single company. A ratified international standard already defined a terrain node holding four child addresses in a quadtree.
tooltips.geo.indoor: Indoor mapping is a machine-readable description of the inside of a building: rooms, doors, floors, and how they connect. Nothing on this map reaches it. Five subjects are partial, two are absent, and seven are out of scope and hidden. It is one of only two capabilities nothing reaches natively or through an extension. Be precise about the reading: five subjects sense a room live and none writes it down, so under the looser reading, where partial counts, the answer is zero empty capabilities.
tooltips.input.session: This row is starting, running and ending a headset session: the frame loop, the tracked spaces, the views to draw. Seven subjects have it built in, two reach it through a plug-in, three are partial, two are absent, two conflict, and one is out of scope and hidden. Do not read headset support as conformance: Resonite targets vendor runtimes instead, and its lead developer names the standard as future work. This row and the graphics interface row both read supported and do not compose.
tooltips.input.controller: This row is buttons, sticks and the pose of a thing held in the hand. Ten subjects have it built in, two reach it through a package, two are absent, two conflict, and one is out of scope and hidden, so the answer here is settled. The immersive runtime interface makes this an action row rather than a device row: the application declares what it wants to know and the runtime picks the control. That is why input transfers between headsets. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.input.hand: Hand tracking is the pose of every finger joint, used as input with nothing in the hand. Five subjects have it built in, four reach it through extensions or packages, two are partial, two are absent, and two are out of scope and hidden. Four of the claims are extensions rather than core, which is the usual shape for anything a device may or may not have. The ratified cross-vendor extension fixes 26 named joints per hand; the browser module names 25.
tooltips.input.eye: Eye tracking is where a person is looking, used as an input. Three subjects have it built in, three reach it through extensions, one is partial, five are absent, and two are out of scope and hidden. The privacy constraint is what makes it a standards question rather than a feature question: the ratified extension keeps gaze behind the same permission machinery as any other input, and the browser interface stops exposing it during trusted browser screens.
tooltips.input.haptic: Haptics is the buzz in a controller that tells you that you touched something. Six subjects have it built in, one reaches it through the browser's own gamepad specification, four are partial, two are absent, and two are out of scope and hidden. Partial usually means a single pulse with a strength and a duration and no waveform. It is settled at connection time because the sending world does not know what the receiving device can do.
tooltips.input.devcaps: This row is asking a client what it can actually do before sending it something it cannot run. Six subjects have it built in, ten are partial, and three are absent. Partial means the same thing nearly every time: each publishes its own capability list in its own shape, so two implementations agree on the fields and disagree on the values. This is the row a portal handoff needs and does not have. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.logic.script: A scripting runtime is the language the rules of a world are written in: what happens when you pick something up. Nine subjects have it built in, four are partial, three are absent, one conflicts, and eight are out of scope and hidden, because a file format has no execution model. Scripting is engine-bound and deliberately so. The conflict is VRChat, whose dialect, in its own words, follows no version of the language specification it resembles. The RP1 claim has no public source.
tooltips.logic.behaviour: This row is interactivity that travels inside the asset: a door that knows how to open, wherever it is opened. Four subjects have it built in, one reaches it through packages, six are partial, six are absent, two conflict, and three are out of scope and hidden. Get the standing of the extension right: it sits at release candidate, its text merged into the repository, and it was submitted for ratification on 2026-07-16. Submitted is not ratified.
tooltips.logic.sandbox: Sandboxing is running somebody else's code inside your world without it reaching your world. Two subjects have it built in, ten are partial, seven are absent, and one is out of scope and hidden. The absent ones load outside content and add no boundary of their own beyond the browser's or the process's. Partial and absent together say the useful thing: everyone limits guest code somehow and almost nobody writes the limit down, so nothing here can be conformance-tested.
tooltips.logic.agent: Agent integration is an autonomous agent acting inside the world as a participant rather than as a script. Two subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a package, eight are partial, three are absent, and six are out of scope and hidden, because a device interface has no actors. The row is young and thinly scored, and the map records engine services and outside control channels rather than any standard. Partial usually means an authoring tool, not an in-world agent.
tooltips.logic.budget: Resource budgets cap how much memory, time and calls a guest piece of content may use. Four subjects have them built in, three are partial, seven are absent, and two are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones measure cost with profilers and bound nothing. Only closed platforms enforce a budget and no standard defines one, which is exactly the shape of problem a working group can take on: the numbers are published, so the vocabulary is the missing part.
tooltips.persist.world: World state persistence is what is still there when the world restarts: the chair somebody moved, the wall somebody built. One subject has it built in: Roblox, with two documented stores on its own servers. Eight are partial, four are absent, and six are out of scope and hidden. It is one of the nine thin rows, one of five where that closed platform is the only built-in answer, so there is no second one to point at. Persistence is the thinnest region here: four rows, seven reaching claims.
tooltips.persist.inventory: Inventory is the items a person holds, and whether they can take them anywhere. Two subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a package, three are partial, four are absent, one conflicts, and six are out of scope and hidden, because a drawing library holds no items. Use the worked example rather than a hypothetical: Rec Room, which shut down on 2026-06-01, issued items and the currency that bought them itself, and both stopped being spendable on a date.
tooltips.persist.prefs: Preference portability is accessibility settings and comfort options following a person into a world they have never visited. One subject has it built in: Roblox, whose account settings every Roblox experience can read. Six are partial, seven are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. It is one of the nine thin rows, one of five where a closed platform is the only built-in answer, so there is no second one. It is also the cheapest of the five to standardise.
tooltips.persist.content-addr: Content addressing is naming a file by a hash of its own bytes, so the name proves the contents. Two subjects have it built in, seven are partial, eleven are absent, and three are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones name assets by location, so two copies of the same bytes are two different things. One shipped example, with its limit: Resonite names every asset by a hash and serves it over an ordinary web address, unauthenticated, so holding a hash is holding the content.
tooltips.deliver.bundle: A bundle format is the package a person can actually run: the thing a store ships. Start with the three conflicts, Horizon Worlds, Rec Room and VRChat: on those platforms a published world is never a file the creator can hold. Rec Room's own shutdown notice told creators they could not download a working copy of their rooms. Five subjects have it built in, seven are partial, two are absent, and four are out of scope and hidden. The RP1 claim has no public source.
tooltips.deliver.cdn: Content delivery is getting the assets to a hundred thousand clients without the origin server melting. Two subjects have it built in, two reach it through engine services, eight are partial, one is absent, one conflicts, and three are out of scope and hidden. Partial nearly always means a well-behaved client of somebody else's infrastructure. It belongs on an interoperability map because delivery is where a client-server world's real cost sits, and it constrains what a portal can promise.
tooltips.deliver.version: Versioning and update is shipping a change without breaking what people already made. Fourteen subjects have it built in, one reaches it through a package, seven are partial, one is absent, and three conflict, so the answer here is settled. Say the conflicts as the platforms state them: changing editor version stops uploaded content loading, and adding a networked component makes the next build incompatible with instances already running. TeleportXR's claim has no public source.
tooltips.deliver.conformance: Conformance testing is a test suite that proves an implementation matches the specification, rather than a claim that it does. Seven subjects have it built in, eleven are partial, eight are absent, one conflicts, and three are out of scope and hidden. The absent ones publish no specification to match. The older ratified scene standard carries a conformance clause covering files, generators and readers with a base profile, while the newest scene specification says its own tests will be made available. The Universal Manifest claim has no public source.
tooltips.rp1: RP1 Spatial Fabric treats a place in three dimensions as a document with a web address: a signed manifest, an engine that reads it, and a browser that opens it. The register records a project from RP1, version 0.3.0 dated 2026-07-16, licensing mixed: the engine is permissive, the browser proprietary. There is no format specification and no conformance suite, so compatible with this format has no testable meaning. Scored on 30 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 40 sources, nine of them local files rather than public pages.
tooltips.teleportxr: TeleportXR is a session protocol rather than a file format: a server is the authority for a live simulation, and each client receives only the slice of state it needs. The register records a project from Teleport XR Ltd, MIT licence, draft 0.9 dated 2026-09-03. Its own documents say Teleport has no file format, and that its network is part of the Internet but not part of the Web. Scored on 43 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 25 sources, two of them local files.
tooltips.wow: Web of Worlds is a Metaverse Standards Forum direction for making virtual worlds addressable and linkable with ordinary web machinery. The register records a Forum project, whitepaper 0.0.1 dated 2026-06-02. Its whole normative surface is three small interface files and a table of five requirements; units, scale, up axis, coordinate frames, signatures and portal destinations are absent rather than wrong. It is one of four subjects reaching the addressing row natively. Scored on 34 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 14 sources, four of them local.
tooltips.iwps: Disclosure first: the owner co-chairs the technical group of OMA3, which publishes this. The Inter-World Portaling System is a draft protocol for one narrow job, moving a person from one virtual world to another over two ordinary web calls. The register records a draft 0.3 from OMA3, dated 2025-09-25, and the text has not moved since. Its asset transfer, look-and-feel and payment sections each read to be decided. Scored on 30 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 2 sources; 59 rows were never assessed.
tooltips.um: Disclosure first: this is the owner's own draft, and the only native answer on two of the map's nine thin rows. Universal Manifest is a signed identity envelope carrying who a person is, what they consent to, and pointers to things they own. The register records a draft 0.4 from the Universal Manifest Working Group, dated 2026-07-09. Its reciprocal binding mode carries a live specification defect whose exposure is governed by adoption, not elapsed time. Scored on 24 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 20 sources, eight local files.
tooltips.c2pa: C2PA Content Credentials are signed statements bound to a file's bytes, recording who made content and what was done to it. The register records a standard from C2PA, open, shipping. No three-dimensional format appears in its supported-format list, so a model can only be covered by a separate sidecar manifest that nothing keeps attached. Its identity and its training-and-data-mining assertions left the core in January 2024 and now belong to another body. Scored on 10 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 4 sources; 79 were never assessed.
tooltips.did: A decentralized identifier is a name its own controller holds, rather than one an account provider issues. The register records a ratified 1.0 from the World Wide Web Consortium, dated 2022-07-19. It settles the identifier, the document it resolves to, and which key serves which purpose, then stops: no claims about a person, no handover protocol. The method register held 267 entries on 2026-08-12, and the newer revision has not advanced past candidate stage. Scored on 11 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 3 sources; 78 were never assessed.
tooltips.ieee2874: IEEE 2874 Spatial Web is a reference model rather than something an engineer can build against: its own project record says it defines requirements for implementation specifications still to be developed. The register records a standard from IEEE, board-approved 2874-2025 dated 2025-05-28. Say board-approved rather than published, and take that date from the standards body's own catalogue, which differs by one day from the originating foundation's page. Its normative text is sold and was never read here, so all 9 scored rows are second-hand; 80 rows were never assessed.
tooltips.mpeg-arf: MPEG-I Avatar Representation Format is a draft international standard for carrying a person's avatar between applications, and it is not finished. The register records a draft 23090-39 DIS from ISO-IEC SC29, dated 2026-07-31, when its ballot passed; publication is expected early in 2027. It is not the first formal standard to try this. Its matrices are transposed against the common transfer format, so a straight copy loads without error and places the avatar wrongly. All 15 scored rows are second-hand; 74 were never assessed.
tooltips.mpeg-audio: MPEG-I Immersive Audio is a finished international standard for immersive sound in virtual and augmented spaces. The register records a ratified 23090-4:2025 from ISO-IEC SC29, dated 2025-11-03. State the evidence limit before the claim: the normative text is sold rather than published, so all 12 scored rows are second-hand. They rest on the three sources the database holds for it, which are the catalogue record, the group's own standard page and the white paper. It defines nothing about carrying live voice between participants. Another 77 rows were never assessed.
tooltips.mpeg-scene: MPEG-I Scene Description is a published international standard that defines no scene format of its own; it specifies extensions to an existing one, plus an interface between a client's drawing part and its fetching part. The register records a ratified 23090-14:2025 from ISO-IEC SC29, dated 2025-11. What it brings is timed media: video as a texture, spatial audio with reverberation, refilling buffers, scene updates as samples, and a viewpoint that moves. Scored on 24 of the 89 rows, 16 verified and 8 second-hand, on 18 sources; 65 were never assessed.
tooltips.3dtiles: OGC 3D Tiles streams very large geographic three-dimensional data by tile, and it is the only ratified document on this map that solves that. The register records a ratified 1.1 from the Open Geospatial Consortium, dated 2023-01-12; approval was 2022-12-17. Get its class right: it is a Community Standard submitted by one company, not an Implementation Standard. Version 1.1 already deprecated its own four original tile formats. Scored on 19 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 4 sources; 70 were never assessed.
tooltips.geopose: OGC GeoPose is a small finished standard saying where something is on Earth and which way it faces, in an exchangeable form. The register records a ratified 1.0 from the Open Geospatial Consortium, dated 2023-09-08; the document records approval on 2022-06-20 separately. It is a data structure, not a service: the word resolve does not appear in it. Its published latitude rule is missing a minus sign, so read literally it permits only the north pole. Scored on 12 rows, all verified, on 1 source; 77 were never assessed.
tooltips.usd: OpenUSD Core Specification standardizes the machinery for combining a scene out of many files, not what you put inside. The register records a ratified 1.0.1 from the Alliance for OpenUSD, dated 2025-12-12; there is no 1.0.0. The ratified core defines no unit of length and no up axis, both appearing only inside example code, so two conforming files can disagree about scale and orientation. Its licence forbids distributing a derivative work. Scored on 18 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 2 sources; 71 were never assessed.
tooltips.openxr: OpenXR is the settled way for an application to talk to a headset or a pair of glasses: the session, the frame loop, the tracked spaces, the views to draw and the input. The register records a ratified 1.1.62 from Khronos, dated 2026-07-31. Two builds of the same document exist, one carrying ratified extensions and one carrying all registered extensions, and the second says of itself that it is not a ratified specification. Never cite an extension without its stage. Scored on all 89 rows, all verified, on 6 sources.
tooltips.vrm: VRM is a humanoid avatar format built on the common transfer format: one added extension and a changed file suffix. The register records a ratified 1.0 from the VRM Consortium, dated 2022-09-22. It adds what the base format lacks: named human bones with fixed parentage, a normative rest pose, facial expressions for moods, speech and gaze, and machine-readable permission data. It is the only native answer on two of the nine thin rows, one being licence metadata. Scored on 30 rows, all verified, on 16 sources; 59 were never assessed.
tooltips.vc: A verifiable credential is a signed statement made by one party about a subject that a third party can check without asking the first party. The register records a ratified 2.0 from the World Wide Web Consortium, dated 2025-05-15. It does not require decentralized identifiers, which are one example among plain identifiers and web addresses, and selective disclosure is the issuer's choice at issuing time rather than something a holder can add later. Scored on 11 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 2 sources; 78 were never assessed.
tooltips.webgpu: WebGPU is a low-level interface that lets a web page drive the graphics processor for drawing and for general computation. The register records a candidate, CR Draft, from the World Wide Web Consortium, dated 2026-08-20. It is not finished: the main specification and its separate shading language specification are both Candidate Recommendation Drafts, so nobody should cite it as a completed recommendation. It does ship by default in all three browser engines, with gaps on some system and hardware combinations. Scored on all 89 rows, all verified, on 4 sources.
tooltips.webxr: WebXR Device API is the way a web page reaches a headset or a phone's pass-through camera. The register records a candidate, CR Draft, from the World Wide Web Consortium, dated 2026-06-09. It is not finished: no part of this family has reached full Recommendation, and its modules sit at very different stages. Browser support is not settled: it ships by default in one engine family, in a second only on a headset platform, and a third never has. Scored on all 89 rows, all verified, on 18 sources.
tooltips.x3d: X3D is the oldest and widest thing on this map: a published international standard in its fourth edition. The register records a ratified 4.0 from Web3D and ISO-IEC, dated 2023-12. It already contains what newer formats are still drafting: rigid body physics with six joint types, spatialized sound, a bound humanoid skeleton, a geospatial component, networked state sharing, and a conformance clause. Physics and simulation sit in the fullest profile, and its sound clause never mentions occlusion. Scored on 44 rows, all verified, on 15 sources; 45 were never assessed.
tooltips.gltf: glTF is the settled way to hand a three-dimensional model from one tool to another. The register records a ratified 2.0.1 from Khronos, dated 2021-10-11. One split governs every row: the shape of a thing and how its surface looks are in the ratified core; how a thing behaves is not. Twenty-three extensions are ratified, none of them physics or audio, and there is no avatar extension at any registry stage. Scored on 34 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 13 sources; 55 were never assessed.
tooltips.gltf21: glTF 2.1 is a planned backward-compatible revision of that core, announced on 2026-06-11 and still being written. The register records it as in-development, from Khronos. What exists is draft text for four features on a working branch: a file may reference other files, package them inside itself, carry simple shapes, and hang bounding volumes on nodes. The published registry has no 2.1 document, and no primary source states a ratification date. Scored on 28 of the 89 rows, all verified, on 13 sources; 61 were never assessed.
tooltips.godot: Godot is a free and open source game engine under a permissive licence. The register records a shipping 4.7.2 from the Godot Foundation, dated 2026-08-18. Its distinctive idea explains its composition score: everything is a node in a tree, any tree saves as a scene, and any saved scene sits inside another as one node. A gap here is usually a gap in the default build, since most subsystems sit behind a public interface. Scored on 79 rows, 73 verified and 6 second-hand, on 84 sources; 10 were never assessed.
tooltips.unity: Unity is a commercial real-time three-dimensional engine and editor whose own files are not an exchange format: scenes, prefabs and asset bundles are read only by Unity. The register records a shipping engine from Unity Technologies. One qualifier applies to most of its rows: almost everything a shared world needs beyond the base editor arrives as a separate installable package, so a claim that Unity supports something is usually a claim about a package, not the engine. Scored on all 89 rows, 71 verified and 18 second-hand, on 91 sources.
tooltips.unreal: Unreal Engine is a source-available real-time engine from Epic Games, scored here at version 5.8. The register records a shipping 5.8, dated 2026-06-17. Correct the old line: version 6 has not shipped. What shipped that day was 5.8, the version 6 plan was announced the same day with early access targeted at late 2027, and there are no version 6 documentation pages. Verse runs only inside Epic's own service. Scored on 79 rows, 46 verified and 33 second-hand still needing primary sources, on 55 sources; 10 were never assessed.
tooltips.babylonjs: Babylon.js is an open-source web rendering engine and application framework from Microsoft and community contributors, covering far more than drawing: the scene graph, animation, skinning, model reading and writing, and a full immersive session stack. The register records it as shipping under a permissive licence. Physics is not in the engine at all, so every physics row is delivered by a plug-in wrapping an outside engine, and several other claims belong to official sibling packages rather than the core. Scored on all 89 rows, all verified, on 75 sources.
tooltips.cesiumjs: CesiumJS draws a whole-Earth globe and streams very large geographic three-dimensional data into a browser. The register records a shipping library from Cesium GS. The company behind it created the tiled format the Open Geospatial Consortium later approved as a community standard, and this library is its reference implementation. It carries no physics, no audio and no multi-user networking, and its stereoscopic mode does not use the immersive web interface, so it is not a headset runtime. Scored on all 89 rows, all verified, on 57 sources.
tooltips.playcanvas: PlayCanvas is two things under one name: an open-source runtime under a permissive licence, and a hosted editor and publishing service. The register records it as shipping. The runtime draws well and both reads and writes the common transfer format, but physics ships as components that stay inert until the application separately loads an outside WebAssembly library, and the runtime carries no networking and no identity at all. Reading other formats and producing a runnable package are hosted-editor jobs. Scored on all 89 rows, all verified, on 64 sources.
tooltips.threejs: Three.js is an open source library for drawing three-dimensional scenes in a browser, and it is a library rather than an engine. The register records a shipping library from mrdoob and contributors. One split governs most of its rows: every file format reader and writer, all post-processing on the main path, the camera controls and the physics wrappers sit in the addons folder as optional modules rather than in the core build. Scored on 69 rows, all verified, on 64 sources; 20 were never assessed.
tooltips.horizon: Horizon Worlds is a closed social platform one company builds and runs; a published world is never a file a creator holds. The register records it as shipping, from Meta. The unusual positive: the editor writes a whole world back out as a common interchange file, so geometry can return; gizmos, scripts, lighting and colliders stay behind. It has more recorded conflicts than any other subject, so read the notes, not the colour. Scored on 88 rows, 64 verified and 24 second-hand, on 43 sources; one was never assessed.
tooltips.recroom: Rec Room was a social virtual world platform that closed permanently on 2026-06-01, taking its website with it; the register records it as shutdown on that date. It stays on the map as the clearest example of what a closed platform costs when its operator stops: every address ever minted became unresolvable on one day, the currency stopped being spendable, and its shutdown notice told creators they could not download a working copy. Scored on 44 rows, 31 verified and 13 second-hand, on 12 sources; 45 were never assessed.
tooltips.resonite: Resonite is a social virtual world platform on a live, fully reflective data model: a wristwatch and a world are the same kind of object. The register records it shipping, from Yellow Dog Man Studios. Traffic runs one way: it reads dozens of formats and writes almost none back; exported skinned meshes lose bone weights and shape keys. It does not run on the immersive session standard. Every asset is named by an unauthenticated hash of its bytes. Scored on all 89 rows, 78 verified, 11 second-hand, on 100 sources.
tooltips.roblox: Roblox is a proprietary platform and, by a wide margin, the best documented subject here. The register records it shipping, from Roblox Corporation. Its units differ from metres: the length unit converts to 28 centimetres, the mass unit to 21.952 kilograms, gravity to about five and a half times Earth. The engine converts nothing, so a metre-authored scene arrives wrongly sized and falling at the wrong rate. It is the only native answer on five of the nine thin rows. Scored on all 89 rows, all verified, on 88 sources.
tooltips.vrchat: VRChat is a social world platform on a game engine; worlds and avatars are authored there and uploaded. The register records a shipping platform from VRChat Inc. An upload becomes an asset bundle keyed to one editor version and one platform; the widely adopted portable avatar format is not supported, with no export. Its own documentation states that persistent data cannot be shared between different worlds, so any portal-handoff proposal must answer that. Scored on 86 rows, 70 verified and 16 second-hand, on 69 sources; three were never assessed.
tooltips.omb: The Open Metaverse Browser is the Forum's own neutral client for spatial content: a working browser with a downloadable binary, a module interface and five language bindings. The register records a Forum project, preview 0.3.0 dated 2026-07-16. The governance split matters: the engine is the Forum's, permissively licensed, while the browser a person runs is the vendor's, proprietary with all rights reserved. Signature verification is called and its result discarded, and there is no resource budget. Scored on 65 rows, all verified, on 46 sources; 24 were never assessed.
tooltips.render: Rendering and presentation covers turning a scene into pixels. It opens at Rasterization pipeline and closes at Camera and viewpoint model. Just outside sits Material exchange, which carries a material between two different renderers and belongs to Scene and assets. The heading holds ten capabilities, nine settled when a project is built and one settled when two systems connect. The fourteen headings are this project's own cut of the ground: no file defines them, and the page never shows which plane a heading belongs to.
tooltips.scene: Scene and assets covers what a world is made of and how it moves between tools. It opens at Scene graph model; Bundle format, which packs a runnable experience, sits just outside under Packaging and delivery. It holds fourteen capabilities, all settled when a project is built. Three ratified standards define a scene graph natively, so what cannot be replaced is each engine's own graph, not the capability itself. Rights and licence metadata has a single native claimant. The fourteen headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.avatar: Avatars covers the portable description of a person in a world. It opens at Avatar body format; Skeleton and rig definition, the general rig, sits just outside under Scene and assets. It holds seven capabilities, four settled when a project is built and three when two systems connect. Facial expression standard and Attachments and wearables each have one native claimant. Do not call the current draft international standard the first formal standard for carrying an avatar between worlds. The fourteen headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.physics: Physics and simulation covers what moves by rule rather than by script. It opens at Rigid bodies; Morph targets and blend shapes sits just outside under Scene and assets. It holds seven capabilities, six settled when a project is built and one when two systems connect. Do not say nobody has standardized physics: a ratified international scene standard has defined rigid bodies since 2008, in a clause still in its current fourth edition, December 2023. The headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.audio: Audio covers sound placed in a world and carried to the people in it. It opens at Positioned audio sources; Media transport, which carries live audio and video for a session, sits just outside under Networking and session. It holds six capabilities, four settled when a project is built and two when two systems connect. The immersive audio standard's normative text is sold rather than published, so every one of its rows here is second-hand, never verified. The headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.net: Networking and session covers what two running systems agree on while connected. It opens at State replication; Immersive session lifecycle, the device-side session, sits just outside under Input and devices. All twelve of its capabilities are settled when two systems connect. Do not say nothing names a place and resolves it: four subjects reach world addressing natively and seven more in part. Shared state between running instances was also called empty when a ratified clause already covered it. The headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.identity: Identity, trust and rights covers who a person is and what they may do. Say the conflict of interest first: two of its capabilities are reached only by Universal Manifest, this group's co-chair's own draft. It opens at Identity root; Provenance and authorship sits just outside under Scene and assets. All seven capabilities are settled when two systems connect, three of them have a single claimant, and Rights enforcement is reached by nothing on the map. The headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.geo: Spatial and geospatial covers where something sits on the Earth. It opens at Geospatial pose; Transforms and coordinate convention, the scene's own axes, sits just outside under Scene and assets. It holds seven capabilities, three settled when a project is built and four when two systems connect. Nothing on the map reaches Indoor mapping. The geospatial pose standard carries a typo in a normative requirement, and the tiled terrain standard is a Community Standard, not an Implementation Standard. The headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.input: Input and devices covers how a person reaches into a world through hardware. It opens at Immersive session lifecycle; Session establishment, which is joining a running world over a network, sits just outside under Networking and session. All six capabilities are settled when two systems connect. Do not read conformance to the immersive session standard from the fact that a platform supports headsets: at least one large social platform targets vendor runtimes instead. The headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.logic: Logic and behaviour covers the rules of a world and what runs them. It opens at Scripting runtime; Trigger volumes, regions that fire events when entered, sits just outside under Physics and simulation. It holds five capabilities, four settled when a project is built and one when two systems connect. This project's own research once called the interactivity extension ratified. It is a release candidate, submitted on 16 July 2026. The headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.persist: Persistence and storage covers what survives after a session ends. It opens at World state persistence; Content delivery sits just outside under Packaging and delivery. It holds four capabilities, one settled when a project is built and three when two systems connect. It is the thinnest region on the map: its four capabilities hold seven claims of built in or through an extension between them, and World state persistence and Preference portability have one claimant each. The headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.deliver: Packaging and delivery covers turning a project into something a person can run and getting it to them. It opens at Bundle format; Asset container format, the file that carries a model between tools, sits just outside under Scene and assets. It holds four capabilities, three settled when a project is built and one when two systems connect. Nobody in this stack publishes a conformance suite, so its absence is not a criticism this project can make loudly. The headings are this project's own cut, defined in no file.
tooltips.level.native: Built in means the subject specifies or carries out this capability itself, in its core: not through a plug-in and not on a roadmap. 458 claims on the map carry it, so a solid block is the strongest thing the map says. It stays a claim about one subject on its own. Two subjects both marked built in are not promised to work together, and the graphics interface and immersive session rows are the worked pair that both read supported and do not compose.
tooltips.level.via-extension: Through an extension means the capability arrives in a named extension, plug-in, module or optional profile, and the note always names which one. 92 claims carry it. The distinction earns its own mark because an extension can be unratified, sold by one vendor, or absent from the registry it is supposed to sit in. Submitted is not ratified and a review draft is two stages below ratified, so a hatched block is never proof of a ratified answer.
tooltips.level.partial: Partial means some of the written definition is met and some is not, and the rule requires the note to say which part is missing. 442 claims carry it, the second largest group on the page, so most of the map's real detail sits here. Partial also changes the answer to how empty a row is: under the reading where partial counts, no capability on this map is unreached. Say which reading you are using before you use the word empty.
tooltips.level.none: Absent means the capability is in scope for something like this subject and is genuinely not there. It is a judgement, not an oversight, and it is not the same as out of scope, which the page does not draw at all. 337 claims carry it. Absence is the weaker half of the record: every claim that a capability is present was checked, and rows that could not be confirmed always asserted absence, never presence. State an absent cell as this project's reading, not as fact.
tooltips.level.conflicts: Conflicts means the subject does this in a way that will not work with the common approach, and the note has to say how. 50 claims carry it. Every one is quoted from the subject's own documentation, which makes them the most concrete material on the map and the easiest to overstate. Quote the documentation rather than describe it, and never present a conflict as bad faith: a platform is entitled to its own design.
tooltips.level.out-of-scope: Out of scope means the subject is not the kind of thing that would do this. It is a real answer rather than a blank. 370 claims carry it, and the page draws none of them: a style rule hides every one and the legend has no key for it, so a reader cannot tell a scoped-out subject from an unscored one. Those hidden claims still count inside the claims total at the top. Nothing visible on the page can carry this note until the page draws the level.
tooltips.confidence.verified: Verified means somebody on this project read the primary source and can quote it.
