Primary means specification text, an official registry, official documentation or the project's own repository, never a blog, marketing page or encyclopedia. 10,383 of the 10,659 claims hold it. The page prints the word only inside the claim detail a click opens, never on the cell itself, so the strength of a claim is invisible where it is drawn. Verified is a claim about having read something, so check it before repeating it.
tooltips.confidence.reported: Reported means a credible second-hand source says so and no primary source could be reached. On this map the usual reason is that the normative text is sold rather than published. 165 claims hold it, and they cluster on systems whose documentation is closed or sold: Unreal Engine 33, Horizon Worlds 24, Unity 18, VRChat 16, and 35 across the three immersive media parts. The page prints the word only inside the claim detail, never on the cell. Say sold, not published, before somebody asks.
tooltips.confidence.unverified: Unverified is the third value in the scoring rules. It means somebody believed a claim and could not confirm it, and the rule prefers leaving such a row out rather than writing it down. The database holds 141 of them, against 10,383 verified and 135 second-hand. Every one of them asserts that something is absent, never that something is present, which is what makes the gaps view worth trusting. The page prints confidence only inside the claim detail.
tooltips.filter.all: Everything is the default. It shows all 89 capability rows for whichever subjects are switched on, and the page opens with every subject on, so the first thing anybody sees is every row at once. Several runtimes are scored on all 89 rows and most of the ratified standards on fewer than forty, so a page that looks empty on the standards side measures how much has been scored, not what exists. Nothing on disk records why these seven buttons and not others.
tooltips.filter.overlap: Overlaps keeps a row when two or more of the subjects currently switched on score it built in or through an extension. That is the overlap question the map exists to answer, and which rows appear depends entirely on which subject chips are on. An overlap here means two or more claimants, not disagreement: nothing in this test says the two agree with each other, and a recorded conflict is a separate button. Nothing on disk records why these seven buttons and not others.
tooltips.filter.gap: No native or extension support recorded keeps a row when no subject switched on has a native or extension claim, and at least one has a recorded claim other than out of scope. A row can still have partial support. A subject with no recorded claim is unscored, not known to lack support. Rows with no checked claims are excluded.
tooltips.filter.conflict: Recorded conflicts keeps a row where a switched-on subject is scored at the conflicts level: the subject's own documented behaviour clashes directly with the common approach. 50 claims across the map carry it, and every one is quoted from the subject's own documentation. That makes them the most concrete material here and the easiest to overstate, so quote the documentation rather than describe it. Nothing on disk records why these seven buttons and not others.
tooltips.filter.connect: Protocol — agreed when systems connect keeps a row whose binding is connect: the answer is agreed between two systems when they connect, rather than fixed when the content is made. 88 of the 175 capabilities are bound this way, and this filter is the closest thing the page has to a view of the interoperability problem. The binding is a judgement made when the capability list was written. No file records why any single row was bound one way, so be ready to defend a particular case.
tooltips.binding.format: Format is one of two words in the narrow column beside each capability. It says the answer is fixed when the content is made, so a standard for it is a file or engine question. 87 of the 175 capabilities carry it. How a mesh is encoded is the clear case, chosen once by whoever made the file. Format is a claim about when the choice is made, not about how hard the work is, and no file records why any row was bound this way.
tooltips.binding.protocol: Protocol is the other word in that column, printed in its own colour. It says the answer is agreed between two systems when they connect, so a standard for it is a wire question rather than a file question. 88 of the 175 capabilities carry it, including every row under Networking and session and under Identity, trust and rights. Who owns an object is the clear case. Protocol does not mean optional, and no file records why any row was bound this way.
tooltips.count.claims: A claim is one subject scored against one capability. With every subject switched on the map holds 10,659 of them. The number follows the chips: switch a subject off and its claims leave the total. 6,161 claims are scored out of scope and a style rule hides every one, so the number is larger than anything visible: anybody counting the blocks on screen will reach 4,498. Nothing on the page says what it counts, which is why this note exists.
tooltips.count.sources: This counts distinct sources behind the claims of the subjects switched on, not citations: 2,687 with every subject on, made up of 2,664 primary, 17 pieces of local evidence and 6 second-hand. There are 15,199 quotes against those 2,687 sources, because one source supports several claims and one claim sometimes quotes one source twice. The 17 local items are files on the owner's own machine, cannot be shown to anyone else, and belong to four subjects. The page never says what the number counts.
tooltips.count.conflicts: A conflict is a claim scored at the conflicts level: the subject's own documented behaviour clashes directly with the common approach. There are 50, each quoted from the subject's own documentation. They cluster on the five platforms, which carry 33 between them. Use one word for it. The meeting material and the corrections file both call the same thing a collision, so a reader who meets both words will think the page holds two measures. The page never says what the number counts.
tooltips.count.unverified: This number counts recorded claims marked unverified among the subjects switched on. It does not count omitted claims or unscored cells. Unverified describes the confidence in a recorded claim, not whether a subject supports the capability.
tooltips.count.subjects: The left number is how many subject chips are switched on; the right is how many exist. The page opens with all 35 on, because every subject carries at least one score. Since WO-026 the three numbers to its left move with it: claims, sources and conflicts count only the subjects on screen, so the whole line describes the selection rather than the database. The page never says what the numbers count.
tooltips.chipgroup.all: All subjects is a control, not a category. Clicking it turns every subject on, or turns them all off if they are already all on. The page opens with all 35 on. It looks like a group heading and behaves like a switch, which is the one thing to know about it. The small square to its left reports the state of the whole set: filled when every subject is on, part filled when some are, and empty when none are.
tooltips.chipgroup.msf: Read the label with care. None of these six is a Metaverse Standards Forum standard, and two are drafts from bodies this group's co-chair belongs to: Universal Manifest, the co-chair's own draft, is the only claimant of two capabilities on this map. The six are RP1 Spatial Fabric, TeleportXR, Web of Worlds, Inter-World Portaling System, Universal Manifest and the Open Metaverse Browser, named one by one in the generator, because they are the work this group is being asked to look at.
tooltips.chipgroup.standard: Standards holds the published and drafted specifications, seventeen of them. Membership comes from the register's kind column, not from a judgement about quality. The heading flattens a wide range: the seventeen sit at six different statuses, from ratified international standards to one specification still in development. Always give the status with the name, because the single word Standards will otherwise be heard as ratified for all seventeen.
tooltips.chipgroup.game-engine: Game engines holds the three engines a team would actually build in: Godot, which is open source; Unity, which is commercial; and Unreal Engine, whose source is available under its publisher's own terms. Unreal reaches 130 of the 175 capabilities, Unity 123 and Godot 98, so the three of them fill much of the page. That breadth measures how much has been scored, not who covers the ground best.
tooltips.chipgroup.web-runtime: Web runtimes holds four things that run in a browser: Babylon.js, PlayCanvas, Three.js and CesiumJS. Two of them, Three.js and CesiumJS, describe themselves as libraries rather than engines, so a supported claim here often means an optional module the application has to load itself rather than something in the core build. Babylon.js reaches 95 of the 175 capabilities, PlayCanvas 83, Three.js 75 and CesiumJS 63, so they take up much of the page.
tooltips.chipgroup.platform: Platforms holds five closed social worlds, things you visit rather than things you build with: Horizon Worlds, Rec Room, Resonite, Roblox and VRChat. Rec Room closed on 1 June 2026 and stays in the map as evidence, so this is not a group of five live services. Between them they carry 33 of the map's 50 recorded conflicts, each quoted from the platform's own documentation, which makes this the most concrete evidence on the page.
tooltips.filter.thin: Only one system has it keeps a capability where exactly one of the subjects switched on scores it built in. With all 35 subjects on it returns nine rows: Roblox is the sole answer on five of them, VRM on two and Universal Manifest on two. That is the sharpest view on this page, a capability the whole map rests on one implementation for. Which rows appear depends entirely on which chips are on.
tooltips.filter.hasentry: Only rows someone has filled in is a toggle rather than a choice: it combines with whichever other button is on. It hides a capability where none of the subjects switched on scores it as anything but out of scope, so the nothing checked here yet rows and their blank space go. With all 35 subjects on it hides nothing, because every row has an entry; switch down to the Forum group and 71 of the 89 rows remain.
tooltips.row.scored: The line N of M subjects checked here compares recorded claims with the subjects switched on. N counts those with a claim other than out of scope, including recorded absence. M counts all subjects switched on. A subject with no recorded claim does not count as checked.
tooltips.mode.matrix: Matrix mode is the map as rows: 175 capabilities down the page, and a chip on each row for every subject with a claim there. It holds all 10,659 claims, and any chip opens to the note and the sources behind it. Use it when the question is about one row — who reaches this, at what level, and on whose evidence. It is the only mode that shows the wording of a claim.
tooltips.mode.c4: Diagram mode is the same 10,659 claims drawn as bands of cards, in the hand of the wall map: bands stacked down the page, and curves between them. The subject switches and the filters do the same work in both modes, and the count line above stays live either way. Three levels become a curve — built in, through an extension, and conflicts. Partial is counted on the card instead, because with everything on it would bury the picture.
tooltips.mode.atlas: Atlas mode is the map as a place you walk into: the whole territory is twelve boxes, a box opens to the capabilities inside it, and a capability opens to who reaches it and on what evidence. Routes set the whole view in one click, and the filter and the subjects you have switched on travel with you. Start here when the question is where a thing sits; the matrix is the mode for reading one row across every subject.
tooltips.c4.view.landscape: Landscape is the top level: one band for each group of subject chips, a card for every subject you have switched on, and one band under them for the single stack all of them are measured against. A card says how much of that stack its subject touches at any level, partial included. Unreal Engine reaches 130 of the 175 capabilities, the most of anything on the map. Nothing is joined by a curve at this level.
tooltips.c4.view.groups: Groups is the middle level: one band of twelve cards, one for each capability group. Each card says how many capabilities the group holds, how those split between capabilities fixed when the content is made and capabilities agreed when two systems connect, and how many of the subjects on screen have at least one of them. Persistence and storage is the thinnest: 4 capabilities, and 4 of the 35 subjects have some of it. Click a card to open that group.
tooltips.c4.view.group: A group has two bands. The top one holds a card for every capability that passes the filter, with the tally of claims on it: built in, extension, partial, conflicts, absent. The bottom one holds the subjects that have something to draw. Curves join the two — ink for built in, blue for through an extension, red for conflicts. Partial is counted on the card and never drawn. Hover a card to follow its own curves; click a capability to read its claims.
tooltips.toggle.explanations: This chip turns the written explanations on and off. On, hovering or tabbing to a name, a chip or a number opens a box like this one. Off, no box opens anywhere and no item points a screen reader at one, so the page is quieter to read and to show on a screen. This chip keeps its own explanation either way, and the browser remembers the choice for next time.
tooltips.export: This chip opens three ways to take the map away as a file. Two of them are the whole record, built with the page and kept beside it: every claim as a spreadsheet, and the map as a document to read. The third builds a spreadsheet here in the browser from what is on screen right now. Nothing is sent anywhere.
tooltips.export.csv.all: Every one of the 10,659 claims as a spreadsheet, one row each, whatever is switched on here. A row carries the subject, the capability and its group, the binding word, the level, the confidence, the note, and the addresses of the sources the claim rests on. Local evidence gives its title instead of an address. Comma separated, UTF-8, with a header row.
tooltips.export.md.all: The whole map as a document to read: one table for each of the twelve capability groups, capabilities down the side, all 35 subjects across the top, and one symbol per claim. Under each table, every capability with its binding word and its definition. It carries no notes and no sources; the spreadsheet beside it carries those. Markdown, so any editor opens it.
tooltips.export.csv.shown: A spreadsheet of what is on screen now: the subjects switched on, the rows passing the filter, and nothing else. It is built here in the browser, in the same shape as the whole-record file, and it goes nowhere else. Where this copy of the page cannot save a file, the text opens in a new tab instead, or is copied to the clipboard, and the page says which happened.
tooltips.search: Searches capability names and definitions, subject names and group names. Type to see matches; press Enter to go to the first result and highlight it. Escape clears the field. Matching starts at word boundaries, so hand can find handoff but andoff cannot. If a filter hides the selected result, the view returns to Everything and explains the change.
tooltips.metric.covered: Covered asks, of the rows being measured, how many at least one counted subject has built in, then built in or through an extension, then either of those or partial. Production subjects and All subjects on choose which switched-on subjects count. Must-interoperate rows only keeps the production subjects and narrows the rows to those marked must. A selected certification lane limits the metric to its flagged rows. Each figure is a floor on recorded support, not a verdict that independent systems interoperate.
tooltips.metric.production: Counts only switched-on subjects whose status is shipping, ratified, board-approved or mixed. Subjects with other statuses are left out of these percentages. Switching a subject off removes it from the count. The shares describe recorded support over the rows being measured.
tooltips.metric.all: Counts every subject switched on, whatever its status, including drafts and candidates. The shares use the rows being measured and show the effect of including those additional subjects. A subject switched off is never counted. These percentages do not measure whether independent systems interoperate.
tooltips.comment: This opens the place comments go, already carrying the page name and the exact view you are on, and the address you were looking at. Nothing is sent from this page, nothing is stored here, and no outside service is called until you use it. The button stays hidden until a destination is set. Comments are read and folded into the data every two weeks, and the list of what changed appears on this page.
tooltips.layers: Layers opens the atlas at its top level, where the whole map is twelve boxes and nothing else, which is the place to start if this page is too much at once. The link carries the filter you have chosen, so the picture there opens on the same question you were asking here. It is the same data, drawn as regions rather than rows; come back to this page for the claims and their sources.
tooltips.filter.interop: Must interoperate keeps the 35 capabilities where two independent systems have to agree or a use case fails outright: content moving between tools, an avatar travelling, a person travelling through a portal, an agent taking part and paying. Of the other 54 rows, 46 only degrade without agreement and 8 never leave one system at all. Each value is a judgement made one row at a time, and each row carries the sentence that decided it.
tooltips.metric.must: Counts the rows marked must-interoperate, using the switched-on production subjects. The shares show rows reached by at least one counted subject: built in, then built in or through an extension, then either of those or partial. A selected certification lane limits the rows to that lane. These figures describe recorded capability support, not whether independent systems interoperate.
tooltips.interop.must: This mark says two independent systems have to agree on this row, or one of the four use cases fails outright rather than merely arriving worse. 56 of the 175 capabilities carry it; 95 are marked should and 24 need no agreement at all. Hovering the mark on a row gives that row's own reason. It is a judgement about where a boundary lies, not a measurement, and any single row can be argued.
tooltips.lane.content: The content portability lane: the 22 rows an asset cannot move between tools without, taken from use case U1. It holds must rows only, the ones where the use case fails outright unless two independent systems agree, and it leaves every should row out. Clicking it flags those rows and counts covered over them; it hides nothing. A lane is a bundle of capabilities, not a certification: no badge, no register, and nobody issues anything.
tooltips.lane.avatar: The avatar portability lane: the 19 rows an avatar, its worn items and its expressions cannot travel without, taken from use case U2. It holds must rows only, the ones where the use case fails outright unless two independent systems agree. Clicking it flags those rows and counts covered over them; it hides nothing. A lane is a bundle of capabilities, not a certification: no badge, no register, and nobody issues anything.
tooltips.lane.travel: The world-to-world travel lane: the 20 rows a person cannot cross a portal without and stay themselves, taken from use case U3. It holds must rows only, the ones where the use case fails outright unless two independent systems agree. Clicking it flags those rows and counts covered over them; it hides nothing. A lane is a bundle of capabilities, not a certification: no badge, no register, and nobody issues anything.
tooltips.lane.agent: The agent participation lane: the 12 rows a software agent cannot join a world and act without, taken from use case U4. It holds must rows only, and it is knowingly incomplete: the use case says the agent pays for what it uses, and the map has no payment row yet. Clicking it flags those rows and counts covered over them; it hides nothing. A lane is a bundle of capabilities, not a certification: no badge, no register, and nobody issues anything.
tooltips.metric.lane: Under a lane, covered is counted over that lane's rows alone rather than over all 117 or over the 40 must rows. The subject chips still choose who counts. Read the figure carefully: over a lane, in a database of 46 subjects, it reads 100 percent, because somebody somewhere has each row. The number that means something is the one beside it: how many of the lane's rows two or more systems have built in, which is what a test between two implementations needs.
tooltips.capture: Generation and capture covers making a three-dimensional place, or recording one, and getting the result out again. It opens at World generation from a prompt or an image and closes at Panoramic scene imagery. Just outside sits Gaussian splatting and radiance fields, which is drawing splats rather than carrying them, and belongs to Rendering and presentation. The heading holds seventeen capabilities, twelve settled when a project is built and five when two systems connect.
tooltips.sense: World sensing covers a device perceiving the room it is actually standing in: measuring the shape of it, naming what is in it, reporting how far away things are, and hiding virtual content behind real surfaces. It holds four capabilities, every one settled when two systems connect. It is deliberately not Generation and capture: a phone meshing your living room and a model inventing one are different acts.
tooltips.capture.worldgen: This row asks whether a subject makes a whole three-dimensional place from a sentence or a single picture, rather than reconstructing a place that already exists. Built in means the subject produces the world itself. The second half of the score is what comes out: a scene a receiver can keep and open, or frames it can only watch. Reconstruction from photographs is Photogrammetric object capture, not this row.
tooltips.capture.sim-learned: This row asks whether a model keeps a world going by itself, producing each next moment in answer to what the viewer does, instead of handing a scene to an engine to run. Built in means the model is the simulation. Score its stated limits with it: how far ahead the prediction holds, and what drifts. A system that emits one finished world and stops scores absent here.
tooltips.capture.photogrammetry: This row asks whether a subject turns a set of ordinary photographs of a real object into a textured three-dimensional model. Built in means the subject runs that reconstruction itself, end to end. Reading a model somebody else captured is not this row, and neither is inventing an object from a prompt. What leaves is an ordinary asset, so the container and geometry rows carry it from there.
tooltips.capture.splat-format: This row asks whether Gaussian splat data moves between tools and runtimes as a named format with a written definition a second implementation could read. Drawing splats already in memory is Gaussian splatting and radiance fields; delivering them a piece at a time is Captured-scene streaming. This row is only the file. Built in means the subject writes or reads that named format itself.
tooltips.capture.stream: This row asks whether a captured scene arrives a piece at a time, chosen by region and by detail level, so a viewer starts before the whole of it has come and never holds more than it can draw. Built in means the subject publishes that delivery order. The format the pieces are written in is Splat data interchange format. It is a protocol row: two parties agree it live.
tooltips.capture.volumetric-video: This row asks whether a captured scene that changes over time travels and replays as media rather than as authored geometry. Built in means the subject carries the frames together with the camera calibration and mask metadata a second implementation would need to reproduce the shot. Playing a flat video on a surface is not this row, and authored motion belongs to Animation encoding.
tooltips.capture.point-cloud: This row asks how a set of points, each with a position and zero or more attributes, is encoded and compressed for carrying between systems. Built in means the subject defines or reads such an encoding. Drawing points on screen is Volumetric and point cloud under Rendering and presentation: this row is the file, not the frame. A subject with no point representation at all is out of scope.
tooltips.capture.multiview-depth: This row asks whether a scene travels as several calibrated camera views with per-pixel depth, carrying the camera intrinsics and extrinsics a receiver needs to reproject them. Built in means the subject writes or reads that arrangement whole. Without the calibration the views are pictures rather than a place, so a subject that leaves it out reaches partial at best on this row.
tooltips.capture.novel-view: This row asks whether a subject can produce an image from a viewing position that no capture camera occupied. Built in means the subject synthesises that view itself, by whatever method. It is work inside one system: what crosses to a second system is the picture, which is why the row needs no agreement between two implementations to be useful.
tooltips.capture.4d: This row asks whether a capture that changes over time is carried as one moving thing, so a receiver plays it at the right rate instead of being handed each frame as an unrelated file. Built in means the timing travels with the data. How the frames themselves are coded is Volumetric video capture and playback; this row is whether time survives the trip at all.
tooltips.capture.relight: This row asks whether a captured scene answers the lighting of the place it is dropped into, instead of staying lit as it was on the day it was photographed. Built in means the subject separates the capture from the light that fell on it. It is work the receiving system does, so nothing about the decision crosses a boundary.
tooltips.capture.edit: This row asks whether a captured scene can be changed after it is made — cropped, deleted from, recoloured — in a way that survives export and applies to every frame of a moving capture. Built in means the edits are kept rather than baked into one view. Regenerating the world from a description is Generative editing of a world, which is a different act.
tooltips.capture.gen-edit: This row asks whether a world already made can be changed by describing the change in words or pointing at a region, and grown past its original edges, with earlier versions kept rather than overwritten. Built in means the subject offers that loop. It differs from Editing a capture after the fact: one manipulates the data that exists, the other throws it away and generates again.
tooltips.capture.gen-control: This row asks what a generating system accepts as the specification of the world it should make: a description, reference images with their placement, a panorama, a video, a seed, or uploaded coarse geometry, and in which interchange formats that specification may arrive. Built in means the shape is published and a second tool could write it. It is a protocol row, agreed between two parties.
tooltips.capture.derived-asset: This row asks whether a splat or radiance-field world can be turned into the representations a conventional engine already reads: a collision mesh, a mesh for drawing, a panorama, a video. Built in means the subject exports them and states what each route loses. It is how a generated world reaches an ordinary engine at all, so an absent score here leaves the subject on its own.
tooltips.capture.action-io: This row asks whether an agent's actions — poses, joint or gripper values, camera motion — travel into and out of a system as time-sampled data, with the embodiment, the frame, the units and any normalisation stated. Built in means a second implementation could read them without guessing. Most subjects on this map have no action interface of any kind and are out of scope on this row.
tooltips.capture.panorama: This row asks whether a full 360-degree view of a place travels as an image with its projection stated, so a receiver can use it as a scene, as a backdrop, or as a light source. Built in means the subject writes or reads such an image and names the projection. An unstated projection reaches partial at best, because the receiver has to guess it.
tooltips.sense.mesh: This row asks whether a device builds a geometric description of the space around it from its own sensors — mesh, planes, or a parametric room — while the session runs. Built in means the subject produces one. The second half of the score is whether that description can leave the session it was made in. Inventing a place rather than measuring one is World generation from a prompt or an image.
tooltips.sense.semantics: This row asks whether a real surface, object or pixel is named — floor, wall, sky, road, person — as per-pixel classes or detected objects, in a channel set an application can read by name. Built in means the subject labels the world it sees and the labels carry, so a second system can act on them. Labels only that vendor's own tools understand reach partial.
tooltips.sense.depth: This row asks whether a device reports per-pixel distance from the camera to real surfaces, from a depth sensor or inferred from camera imagery, in metric units. Built in means the subject exposes that map to an application. Depth carried inside a captured scene is Multi-view plus depth; this row is the live measurement of the room the person is standing in.
tooltips.sense.occlusion: This row asks whether virtual content is hidden behind real surfaces, using live depth, a reconstructed mesh, or a blend of the two. Built in means the subject does it without the application writing its own. It is drawn on the device that sees the room, so no agreement between two systems is needed for it to work where it works.
tooltips.render.passthrough: This row asks whether a subject mixes the live camera view of the real room with rendered content, and lets an application control how much of each the viewer sees — including cutting a hole in a virtual environment to let a real object through. Built in means the subject offers that control. It is the receiving system's own presentation and carries nothing across to another.
tooltips.input.face: This row asks whether the user's own facial expression and body pose arrive as a live sensor stream, with the privacy constraints that go with it. Built in means the subject delivers that stream to an application. It is not the format an avatar stores its expressions in, which is Facial expression standard: this row is the sensor, that row is the file.
tooltips.scene.navmesh: This row asks whether a place says where a body may stand, walk and arrive — walkable surface, bounds, spawn points — carried with the scene rather than worked out again by whoever opens it. Built in means those declarations travel in the file. Session handoff and portals needs an arrival point to arrive at, which is why this row stands beside it.
tooltips.logic.namespace: This row asks whether a published unit of world logic has a name that resolves to the same thing forever, and that no second author can ever claim. Built in means the subject operates such a namespace. It is what makes a dependency safe to take from a stranger. A language with modules but no permanent identity reaches partial on this row.
tooltips.deliver.moderation: This row asks what review stands between finished content and the people who will see it, and who performs it. Built in means the subject runs that review and says so. The interoperable half is whether a receiving world can tell what review arriving content has already had, rather than repeating the whole of it blind.
tooltips.geo.map-align: This row asks whether a map of a place is declared as a thing with a version and a lifecycle, and whether the transform that aligns it to another map of the same place is published. Built in means both. Without the transform, two maps of one street put the same content in two positions. Making the map is Visual positioning; this row is saying it exists.
tooltips.geo.coverage: This row asks whether a service, dataset or piece of content declares the geographic area it applies to, in a stated frame, so a client can test whether it is relevant where the client is standing. Built in means the declaration is published and a machine can read it. Without one, a client has to call the service and find out.
tooltips.deliver.extension: An extension adds fields or behavior to a shared format or interface. The contract must identify the extension and say what happens when a receiver does not support it. An optional addition may be skipped; a required one may prevent loading. An arbitrary extra field, with no handling rule, does not establish this capability.
tooltips.deliver.profile: A profile or level names a defined set of requirements. Content can declare the set it needs, and an implementation can declare the set it supports. This helps two systems find a compatible contract. A marketing edition, quality setting, or version number alone is insufficient unless its name carries stated technical requirements.
tooltips.render.color: Color values need an interpretation: primaries, transfer function, and the range a surface can present. Declaring these lets a receiver convert textures and images for its own display. Merely accepting RGB numbers is insufficient. A format may define texture interpretation while leaving display range to the runtime; that narrower support must be stated.
tooltips.scene.metadata: Metadata records facts about a scene or its parts, such as a building classification or a component identifier. The values need declared structure so a different system can read them. This does not by itself establish a shared ontology. Free text, opaque application data, and structured metadata offer different amounts of useful agreement.
tooltips.identity.assurance: A claim may include the evidence used to establish it and the assurance attached to that process. A receiver can then judge whether the evidence is sufficient for its use. A valid signature proves who signed a claim; it does not by itself prove the underlying fact or a particular assurance level.
tooltips.identity.schema: A claim needs agreed names, types, and structural rules. A vocabulary explains what its terms mean, while a validation schema checks how its data is arranged. This row concerns claims about a subject, rather than any scene schema. Schema validation alone does not establish that the claim is true or that its issuer is trusted.
tooltips.identity.unlinkable: Pairwise identifiers use different names for different relationships. Unlinkable presentations aim to prevent separate uses of a credential from being matched together. The remaining risks matter: shared keys, service addresses, timestamps, or unusual attributes may still connect the records. Changing an identifier alone is insufficient evidence of an unlinkable exchange.
tooltips.scene.thumbnail: A thumbnail is an image packaged with an asset or referenced from its metadata. A receiver can show it before loading and rendering the three-dimensional content. This is useful in libraries, avatar selection, and arrival previews. The row does not require generating a thumbnail, and an image texture used on the model is not automatically a preview.
tooltips.identity.encryption: A sender needs the recipient's applicable key material and an agreed algorithm to send confidential information. This row covers how that material and those choices are identified. A signature key is not automatically an encryption key. Content protection flags, encrypted transport, and encryption addressed to a subject are related mechanisms with different scope.
tooltips.identity.key-lifecycle: Identity control may need to move to a new key after routine rotation, revocation, or recovery. Receivers need rules for finding the key that applies to a given verification. A standard can define this discovery while leaving the change procedure to an identifier method. Rotating a local secret alone does not establish portable identity continuity.
tooltips.identity.status: An issued credential can later be suspended, revoked, or assigned another status. A status mechanism tells a receiver where and how to discover that change. Expiry is a separate time limit, and revoking a signing key is not necessarily the same as revoking a credential. The check may use an optional named status scheme.
tooltips.render.ui: This row covers the layout and presentation of two-dimensional interface regions, including their dimensions, alignment, and attachment to a display or scene. It does not prove that a user can enter text or select scene geometry. A local widget library provides interface behavior, while portable interface definitions additionally need a shared representation.
tooltips.sense.lighting: A sensing runtime estimates the illumination around a device and exposes values that content can use for lighting or reflections. Examples include an estimated main light, spherical harmonics, or a reflection map. Authored scene lights are different: they describe the virtual scene. A runtime estimate does not automatically provide a portable lighting interchange format.
tooltips.sense.marker: Marker or image tracking recognizes a known physical target and reports its pose in a runtime reference space. Recognition alone is insufficient if no tracked pose is available. This differs from casting a ray against an estimated surface. A marker dictionary, target image, coordinate convention, and tracking state can each affect compatibility between implementations.
tooltips.deliver.resolve: A scene often contains references to images, geometry, or other files. Resolution turns each identifier into the resource to access, using a base location, an alias table, or a resolver context. This step precedes downloading the data. Resolving a person's identity or a world's address does not automatically resolve scene assets.
tooltips.geo.trajectory: This row covers a sequence or stream of poses tied to time. A pose includes location and orientation, so a list of positions alone is only part of the claim. The time base, reference frame and ordering must be clear enough for the receiver to reconstruct movement. Interpolation is a separate declared choice; sending successive transforms does not prove that two receivers interpolate them alike.
tooltips.input.pointing: This row asks whether pointing input can select content and return the object or geometry that was hit. Examples include a mouse ray, a controller ray or a touch location projected into a scene. A device button event alone is insufficient. Testing the estimated physical room is a different capability. An application may implement this locally without exchanging its picking method with another world.
tooltips.input.text: This row covers character or string entry through an input interface. A text field, an on-screen keyboard or a composition-aware input event may provide it. Rendering letters does not establish text entry, and a physical key code alone does not establish the resulting character. The host may handle language and keyboard details locally while the application receives the entered text.
tooltips.render.layer: A compositor layer is an image surface submitted separately to the display system, with a shape, placement and composition properties. Examples include a quad panel or a cylindrical video surface in a headset. Scene sorting layers and ordinary render passes do not by themselves meet this definition. Support may depend on both the application interface and the device runtime that presents the layers.
tooltips.scene.bounds: Bounds describe the space occupied by content without requiring its full geometry. This row includes their organization for early rejection, traversal or selection. A bounding box computed after loading a mesh demonstrates only part of that purpose. A receiver should be able to use the bounds and their reference frame while deciding which parts of a large scene to request or inspect.
tooltips.scene.collection: A collection identifies a set of scene objects by a name or a membership rule. Consumers can use that set as the target of an operation, such as hiding a group, finding tagged objects or applying a change. A parent-child tree alone does not establish this capability. The membership rule and its evaluation scope matter when another system is expected to select the same objects.
tooltips.scene.constraint: Transform constraints describe how one node's position, rotation or scale follows another node. The description needs an evaluation rule, such as an aim, parent or rotation constraint, plus the relevant parameters. A constraint authored only in an editor is weaker evidence than one evaluated at runtime. Physics joints and baked animation may produce similar motion, but they are distinct mechanisms.
tooltips.scene.timed-media: This row concerns timed audio or video used as part of a scene, together with the synchronization needed to present it there. A video texture establishes media presentation but may leave scene timing to the application. Stronger evidence identifies the playback clock, start time, seeking or synchronization behavior. Transporting a live media stream alone does not establish how it relates to the surrounding scene.
tooltips.sense.play-space: The application receives the usable physical area and floor-relative reference information from its sensing runtime. This can help it place or restrict local interaction. A virtual room boundary, navigation mesh or collision volume is not the physical play area. Support also depends on the runtime and reference-space type; a floor-relative origin without usable-area bounds establishes only part of the row.
tooltips.audio.procedural: Procedural audio generates sound during playback from a synthesis model, supporting data and changing controls. This row requires the model to be exchanged for a receiver to evaluate. An interface that accepts arbitrary audio samples proves local generation but does not by itself carry that model. A recorded sound effect and a model that generates a sound effect at play time are different claims.
tooltips.deliver.protection: Protection signalling identifies the scheme associated with protected content components. It lets a receiver determine which mechanism is needed before attempting access or playback. It does not itself grant rights, deliver a key or prove that the recipient may use the content. General transport encryption is not enough unless the exchanged content also declares the protection information needed by its receiver.
tooltips.geo.pose-graph: This row covers exchanged poses and transforms linked into a chain or graph. The links let a receiver reconstruct related coordinate frames consistently, such as a child's pose relative to a parent frame. A local scene tree shows related transforms but does not automatically prove interchange. The representation must identify the relevant frames, links and transform meaning; time-varying samples are covered separately.
tooltips.geo.zone-event: A published zone-event record identifies a spatial area and associates typed events or summaries with it. The spatial and temporal meaning must be clear enough for another system to interpret the record. A local trigger callback alone is only part of the claim. Stronger evidence shows the exchanged zone identifier, event type and timing, including how a summary relates to the underlying area or interval.
tooltips.identity.consent: This row asks whether permission travels with a subject or its represented data. The grant carries its scope, purpose, validity and withdrawal information so a recipient can evaluate the proposed use. A local checkbox or privacy policy alone does not meet the definition. Carrying consent also does not prove that it was validly obtained or that every recipient correctly enforces it.
tooltips.identity.receipt: An evaluation receipt is a machine-readable record of what a recipient evaluated and what action it took. It may record acceptance, rejection or another decision about a presented subject or request. Any signature or integrity proof must be identified explicitly. A plain log line or a boolean result does not automatically meet the whole definition, and an unsigned receipt should not be described as cryptographic proof.
tooltips.net.admission: Before a person or software agent arrives, a destination can approve or refuse entry and state how long that answer applies. This row concerns that response and its meaning. It does not require the destination to reveal its private decision rules, and it does not replace authentication, credential checks, transport setup, or the later session handoff.
tooltips.render.compute: A graphics or compute interface can run programmable work on the graphics processor without drawing triangles. Examples include updating buffers, processing textures, or simulating particles before rendering. This row measures the interface for dispatch and resource access. A tool that merely uses GPU acceleration does not automatically expose this capability, and support does not establish a portable shader language.
tooltips.render.frame-timing: An immersive application needs to know when its next frame is expected to appear and which view poses correspond to that time. This row covers that coordination between application and display runtime. A frame-rate setting, video timestamp, or fast renderer is insufficient by itself. Those describe rate or performance without defining the predicted presentation and submission contract.
tooltips.render.shader-lang: A portable shader language gives independently built implementations the same rules for reading and executing a shader program. This row concerns the source language and its execution meaning. A material graph, a GPU API binding, or the fact that an engine contains shaders does not by itself satisfy it. Portability must be judged within the language's stated profiles and limits.
tooltips.scene.parametric: Parametric geometry stores curves and surfaces as mathematical descriptions instead of only as sampled triangles. A receiver uses the parameters to evaluate points or create a mesh at the needed detail. This row concerns the carried representation and its meaning. A tool's internal procedural modeling commands, or a mesh exported after tessellation, do not preserve that exact mathematical geometry.
tooltips.scene.particle: A particle effect describes where particles are born and how they move, change, and appear over time. This row asks whether emitter and simulation parameters can travel to a receiving runtime for evaluation. A static cloud of points or Gaussian splats is not an emitter system. Rendering an effect locally also does not prove that its behavior survives exchange.
tooltips.scene.provenance-recovery: An asset can lose its embedded link to an authorship or editing record during copying or conversion. This row covers finding the associated provenance again through a supported fingerprint or watermark. It does not promise that every transformed copy can be matched, that a recovered claim is true, or that a successful match proves the identity of every object in a scene.
tooltips.scene.style: Styling rules can live separately from scene data and select display properties from the data's metadata. For example, a rule could color buildings by height or hide features in a named class. This row concerns those declared rules and the receiver's interpretation. Manual color edits, material assignments, and a general programming language are separate mechanisms.
tooltips.scene.variant: An asset may contain named alternatives, such as a material set, a part configuration, or a visible assembly. This row asks whether those alternatives and their selection mechanism travel with the asset. Generating a fresh variation of an image or world is different. Several unrelated files also do not form a variant system without declared selection semantics.
tooltips.scene.voxel: A voxel volume represents space as cells with properties such as occupancy, density, or color. This row concerns exchanging that volume and its updates as scene content. A renderer or reconstruction algorithm may use a voxel grid internally without exposing such an interchange representation. Point samples, Gaussian primitives, and a surface mesh do not automatically supply the same cell semantics.
tooltips.sense.hit-test: A sensing runtime can test a ray against its estimate of physical surroundings and return where the ray hit. Applications use the resulting pose to place or interact with content. This row concerns real-world estimates, with their tracking and accuracy limits. Selecting a virtual object, sampling a depth value, and intersecting an offline mesh are related but distinct operations.
tooltips.sense.privacy: Sensed data may reveal a room, a person's movement, or other sensitive details. This row covers stated controls on disclosure, such as reducing spatial precision, declaring use and retention, or limiting published poses. The evidence must identify the data and the control. A general account privacy page or ordinary authentication does not alone prove that sensed-data handling is defined.
tooltips.input.event-device: Musical devices and recorded event files can supply typed note and controller events to an application. This row asks for a documented input interface with the identifiers and values needed to interpret those events. Audio samples, microphone capture, arbitrary keyboard presses, and synthesized sound are different capabilities. A receiver must understand the event semantics to act on them consistently.
tooltips.capture.radiance-training: Radiance-field reconstruction fits a scene representation from observed images and camera information. The workflow includes controls over optimization and produces a trained field or Gaussian scene that can later generate views. This row separates learning that representation from drawing an existing one. It also differs from mesh photogrammetry and from generating an object or world solely from a prompt.
tooltips.capture.objectgen: An object generator takes a text or image prompt and produces an individual three-dimensional asset that can be placed in another scene. The output must be geometry or another renderable representation, not only a picture of an object. This row is separate from generating an entire environment, reconstructing a measured scene, or changing the appearance of an existing object.
tooltips.scene.containment: Experience containment asks whether a runtime can host another party's running experience inside a containing world, with its own logic and lifecycle, rather than importing its assets or sending the visitor elsewhere. Native requires three things: a nesting structure with a defined parent relationship, a way to attach behaviour to a contained node, and a stated rule for how messages cross the boundary in both directions. Nesting assets without running contained logic is partial.
tooltips.net.world-coupling: Unattended world coupling asks whether state in one world can cause change in another with no participant present in either. Every other crossing on this map assumes a person carries the change. Native requires two conditions: durable state keyed to the world rather than to a participant, and a defined mechanism by which an external event mutates it while nobody is connected. Player-keyed persistence alone scores none on this row.
tooltips.commerce: Commerce and payments covers paying for things across a boundary and proving what was bought or granted. Payment is the exchange itself; entitlement is the check at the moment of use; a receipt is the portable record of a purchase or grant. Granted authority, network admission and a payment settlement are separate facts, so a subject can reach one without the others. A payment receipt is not a quality verdict, and a licence declaration is not an enforcement test.
tooltips.commerce.payment: This row asks whether a person or an agent can pay for a resource or service through a defined exchange: payment requirements, authorization, and a settlement result for a named scheme, network and asset. An offer or a price list alone does not meet the definition. Paying also does not establish entitlement: that a payment settled says nothing on its own about what the payer may now use.
tooltips.commerce.entitlement: This row asks whether a system checks, at the moment of use, that the person or agent holding something has a current grant to enter, load, use or carry it. The grant binds holder to resource and states expiry, revocation and transfer. Owning a record in an inventory is not the same as a grant another system can check, and declaring a licence is not enforcing it.
tooltips.commerce.receipt: This row asks whether a purchase or a grant leaves a portable, machine-readable record that names the recipient, the resource, the issuer and the time, cites the transaction or grant behind it, and says which fields are signed. A record of what a system decided is a different row, and so is the history of who made an asset. A receipt proves a purchase, not the quality of what was bought.
tooltips.identity.trust-registry: This row asks whether a verifier can discover and apply governed configuration that says which issuers, services or worlds to accept: who governs the list, what an entry means, how entries are added, removed or delegated, and which version applies at a given time. Keys, credentials and trust roots on their own do not choose whom a verifier should accept; that choice is what this row records.
tooltips.logic.agent-authoring: This row asks whether an AI agent, working from outside, can build in a world or platform: create, change and publish its content through a documented interface such as an MCP server, a REST interface, a command line or a published instruction file. It is not the row for agents acting inside a world. An interface that exists only inside one editor's own tools, with no stated scope, does not meet the definition.
tooltips.persist.world-export: This row asks whether a whole place can leave its host: its scenes, assets, behaviour and settings exported and imported in open, documented files, with a statement of what survives if the host closes. Exporting single assets is a different row, and so is surviving a server restart. A download of raw files with no documented structure does not meet the definition.
tooltips.sense.object-track: This row asks whether a system recognises a known physical object from its three-dimensional model, with no markers or prepared images, and reports the object's pose so content stays fixed to it. Tracking printed markers or images is a different row. Recognising a general category of object, without the specific model, does not meet the definition.
tooltips.render.remote: This row records whether a system renders a view on a server from the device's predicted pose and streams the frames back for display. It is recorded descriptively: the Atlas notes which systems do it and does not define an agreement between client and renderer. Streaming ordinary video is a different row, because the view is not driven by the viewer's head.
tooltips.net.live-data: This row asks whether objects in a world can be bound to a live outside source, such as a sensor, a machine controller or a building system, so they follow the real asset, or so the real controller drives the simulated one. Importing a static snapshot of data does not meet the definition. Coupling two virtual worlds to each other is a different row.
tooltips.persist.activity-record: This row asks whether a world can produce a portable statement of what a person did and with what result, readable by a system outside it, such as a learning record store, an employer or an assessor. A score kept only in one vendor's dashboard does not meet the definition. A record of what a system decided about a request is a different row.
tooltips.input.physiological: This row asks whether body signals such as heart rate or skin conductance reach an application as a live stream it can react to, with the privacy terms that go with them. Hand, eye and face tracking are separate rows. A signal that is only logged for later analysis, and never delivered to the running application, does not meet the definition.
